In GTA 6 you've got a partner in crime, and it's quite a bit different than it was when you were pulling heists with Michael, Franklin, and Trevor in the last game. Jason and Lucia aren't just criminal associates, they're a couple, and their romantic relationship is a big part of the story.

Jason and Lucia can grow closer or more distant, depending on your actions, behavior, and choices. That goes for everything from story missions to random criminal acts to everyday interactions and activities. Here's how Jason and Lucia's romance works in GTA 6.

There are four levels to Jason and Lucia's relationship that can change depending on how you play and the choices you make, one being the lowest and four being the highest. Here are the levels:

When you begin playing as a couple in Chapter 1, your relationship is already a strong one, though it'll still take a while to get it up to 4/4, if that's your goal. Certain actions, activities, and choices will raise your relationship score, and you'll know you've done it when you hear a chime and see a +♥️ appear on the right side of your screen.

Here are just a few actions that will add a ♥️ to your score, and there are plenty more:

*Note: You can't initiate sex whenever you want, but there are multiple times in GTA 6 when a sex scene is available to you, signified by double hearts over your home icon on the map or with certain limited-time onscreen prompts.

What leads to a sex scene? In my playthrough, twice these scenes happened while I was showering as one of the characters and the other asked if they could join me (and you can decide to let them or not). Another was after I reached a major milestone by contributing money to our savings account (hey, financial security is a major turn-on in real life, too!) and there was also a sex scene after a sizable heist. All of these happened while I was at a 4/4 "Hot Together" relationship status.

Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

You can also lose hearts from your relationship. This didn't happen often in my playthrough, but here's the ones I experienced:

According to Rockstar, if you want a strong relationship in GTA 6, you have to play both sides of that relationship. That means not just playing as Jason and doing nice things for Lucia, but also playing as Lucia and treating Jason well.

For my playthrough, where I reached the end of the game with a 4/4 "Hot Together" status, my stats show that I played nearly the exact same amount of time as Jason as I did Lucia.

Don't worry, this couple isn't joined at the hip. Both Lucia and Jason have missions, storylines, and activities they can (and are sometimes required to) complete alone. You can play plenty of GTA 6 as just a single character running around without the other, just remember to occasionally spend some time with your partner, respond to their texts, and switch to the other character from time to time.

But trust me, you'll want to spend lots of time together. Their relationship is fun to take part in, from both sides. Plus, doing crimes as a couple really pays off. It's helpful to have an extra set of hands to point guns at people, do crowd control during robberies, shoot out a cop's tires while driving, and carry off more loot than you could handle if you were rolling solo.

I'll be honest: I don't know how the game is different if you have a 4/4 relationship or a 1/4 relationship, because I've only played through the story once at this point, and I kept my relationship as strong as possible for nearly the entire game. We'll know more about the effects of a weak relationship as other players experiment with their relationship status, and we'll update this guide with what we find out.

The GTA 6 Ultimate Edition has a lot of stuff in it, but quite a few of these bonuses only become available at specific points in the story, similar to the Vintage Vice City Pack.

Below I'll lay out each bonus in order of when it becomes accessible in the story, though once you complete mission 11, you should be able to open the main menu store and view these details in each specific entry.

These include the Dinka Endura military motorcycle and the Crest Kayak.

This is an upgrade from Jason's Vapid Ganado vehicle with exclusive mods and classic stylings.

This Lake Leonida mod shop specialises in off-road modifications and hand painted customisation.

Another mod shop, specialising in detailed interiors, exquisite rims, and "donk stylings".

A clothing store in Stockyard that includes various unique looks for Jason and Lucia.

Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

A tattoo parlor, also in Stockyard, with over 50 signature tattoos for Jason and Lucia, designed by real-world art collective, FAILE.

These are apparel and accessories featuring Macca the Gator, a character from a hit Leonida TV Show who you likely will have seen in the game's marketing.

This is a raid on a gang compound that can score you special items and contraband.

These are special skins for Jason's Girardi ES9 Pistol and Lucia's Klose K17 pistol, with engravings. As mentioned, you can get Lucia's in Chapter 2.

A salon in Hamlet that has signature styles, including facial hair options for Jason, plus makeup and nails for Lucia. More styles unlock in Chapter 2, plus even more in Chapter 4.

This is a specialised off-road vehicle for the backwoods of Mount Kalaga and beyond, plus the Paradise Garage in Watson Bay, which features a weapon locker and a secure place to deposit stolen goods that need fencing.

This special set of activities revolves around tracking down and restoring abandoned classic cars and work-in-progress project cars for Wyman.

A Morgan Revolver variant for both Jason and Lucia, including palm-tree etched grips, engravings, and a scope.

This is an additional set of cosmetic options for Jason and Lucia, including basically all aspects of their style; whether outfits, tattoos, or hair and beard options.

This speedboat with a pink and blue palm tree motif comes with an explosive-laden weapons crate.

This signature 90s red and white sports car comes with a retro futuristic livery.

Surprise! We got an early look at GTA 6, too, even though it's only on console.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Grand Theft Auto 6 is not on PC so I can't review it. But somehow I, a member of PC Gamer, got access to GTA 6 before it launched. For the past two weeks I've secretly sunk approximately 100 hours in it (on something called a PlayStation 5) and now, finally, I can talk about it. What a relief.

So this isn't a review, but I can give a verdict of sorts:

It's (mostly) great. But it will be (mostly) so much greater when it comes to PC.

I guess I shouldn't be surprised by just how massive and detailed the world is. It's Rockstar: huge open worlds is what they do, and they've had a decade to do it. But I was stunned when I started playing, and a hundred hours later, I'm honestly still pretty stunned. Rockstar said GTA 6's map is twice as big as GTA 5's map, but it feels twice as big as "twice as big" should feel. It's enormous.

I'm constantly impressed by the macro and micro of it all. I can step back and take in the sheer size and scale of Leonida: the archipelago representing the Florida keys to the south, the vast wetlands standing in for the Everglades, the dense neighborhoods and shining skyscrapers of Vice City, the miles of beaches and forests and industrial areas and state parks. And I can zoom in and admire the tiny details: the carefully placed clutter and photos and belongings in a stranger's apartment, the accurate mating rituals of two great blue herons in the wild, or the font choice on a printout pinned to the wall of an office cubicle instructing employees on breakroom etiquette.

I've lost hours doing nothing but wandering around the world.

I've lost hours doing nothing but wandering around the world, picking a point in the distance that looked interesting and getting distracted by a dozen other things along the way. Exploration is always rewarding: Sometimes, because I find one of hundreds of collectibles hidden throughout the map, but usually because I happen upon an interesting landmark, spot an animal I haven't seen before, stumble into a mysterious scene or sight (I have found many yet haven't unraveled any of them yet), or have a chance encounter with the seemingly inexhaustible supply of "Florida Man"-style weirdos that populate Leonida.

Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

My only issue with the world is that present day Miami doesn't hold a lot of interest for me, pop-culture-wise. New York and Los Angeles are fascinating in any era, and I loved the neon-soaked '80s Vice City from Rockstar's game. But GTA 6's Vice City doesn't quite stand up against Liberty City or Los Santos. I'm not saying it's a bad place to spend time: it's an incredible facsimile of the real Miami, with an intense amount of detail and attention paid to the diversity of the city, like its recreation of Little Havana (called Little Cuba here). But it doesn't grab me the way the cities in the last two GTA games did.

It's stressful being in a new relationship. What if my partner texts me and I don't respond right away? Am I giving them enough attention, or too much attention? If they want to hang out, can I say no if I'm busy doing something else? It's been quite a while since I dated IRL, but the early hours of getting to know Jason and Lucia gave me those early relationship jitters I remember so well.

There are lots of systems in GTA 6 for keeping Jason and Lucia's partnership strong: talking to each other, showing affection, doing activities together, and even committing crimes together will improve their bond. That makes it a little tense when one character wants to do something and you (as the other character) don't.

One day as I was playing as Jason, Lucia texted me because she wanted to talk about our financial future. But I was on a speedboat halfway across the map and I had just spotted what I suspect was one of Florida's many cryptids (which, after 100 hours, I still cannot confirm is actually in the game or not). Was I really supposed to drop everything I was doing?

I dropped everything I was doing. Instead of becoming a renowned cryptid investigator, Lucia and I went to the bank to set up a savings account. Was I happy about it? Hell no. I was annoyed. But that felt real to me—not the cryptid part, but the idea of being responsible to your partner. While playing them, both individually and together, I wanted to be a good partner, and sometimes that meant glumly turning around my stolen speedboat and having a frank talk about money. It's pretty cool that a game about robbing banks and blowing up police helicopters could make me want to be a good boyfriend.

The two of them are a satisfying couple to play in other respects, too. When knocking over a jewelry store or check-cashing place (cute date idea), your partner can perform crowd control, keeping security guards and employees docile, while you smash open display cases, empty cash drawers, and crack the safe in the back room. During story missions, the duo is often split up and you bounce between their perspectives, with Jason shooting his way through a crowd of goons in an office tower to Lucia fighting hand-to-hand several floors above.

I had a really wonderful two weeks of ignoring my real life partner while spending quality time with these two.

But the best moments as a duo are when you're coming up with your own ways to play them as a couple. After trying to rip off narcotics from a gang stronghold, I got into a heavy gunfight in a narrow alleyway, and with Lucia on one side and Jason on the other, I was able to fight my way out. As Lucia I could cover Jason as he advanced, and as Jason I could get better angles on the thugs trying to bring Lucia down. It was fluid, fun, and not part of any main mission, just an organic bit of co-op play with me swapping between them as needed. This was the sort of thing that GTA 5 could only pull off in heavily-scripted story missions with its three characters, but here you really are a dynamic duo.

Even more fun? Just hanging out together as a couple. You can take them both to a store to shop for clothes, then compliment each other on their new looks. Or go on a date and play minigolf while gently trash-talking each other. (Tall Jason to short Lucia: "So, is this, like, regular-sized golf to you?") Hit the night clubs and do some dancing. Buy two ice cream cones, hand one to your partner, and enjoy them together. Even just lying in bed, side-by-side, and scrolling your phones is a warm and fuzzy activity amidst all the crime and bloodshed. It's good stuff. I had a really wonderful two weeks of ignoring my real life partner while spending quality time with these two.

Jason and Lucia are a good match for the more deliberate gameplay of GTA 6. Taking a page from Red Dead Redemption 2, your car is basically now your horse: not just a ride, but a gun locker. No longer can you keep a full arsenal in your weapon wheel or unholster a grenade launcher from your back pocket.

The pair can conceal two handguns in their pants, but "long" guns like shotties and rifles are visible on your back or in your hands. This matters: Even the locals of the gun-friendly Leonida will notice and sometimes panic at the sight of a heavily armed maniac, drawing outright alarm from security guards and cops.

So you'll have to stash those big guns in your car until you need them, along with a few changes of clothes because witnesses to your crimes will tell the cops what you're wearing. This makes even a quick, mindless smash-and-grab feel like a mission with phases and choices: scope it out, plan your moves and escape route, grab your gear, and then afterwards, stow your guns and change clothes once the cops are out of sight. When things go sideways, it can be a lot of fun to scramble your way out of the heat: dumping your big guns in an alleyway and running into a clothing shop to buy some new duds, a hat, and sunglasses, so you don't match the description the cops are looking for.

And while you can't play entirely non-lethally, you can at least play less-lethally. Using your focus meter (bullet time) will highlight your enemies' elbows, knees, hands, shoulders, and other non-fatal places to deposit a bullet, so you can incapacitate them instead of just headshotting them if that's how you want to roll. I did a lot of that in my playthrough, partly to keep Jason and Lucia feeling less like murdering psychopaths so that I could continue to like them as characters, but also because it added an extra challenge: aiming carefully at joints instead of just popping lead in every dome I see.

Playing less lethally is another way GTA 6 makes the near-constant violence a bit less mindless, though trust me, my body count was still pretty high by the end of the main story. It's hard to non-lethally shoot down a helicopter with a grenade launcher from the back of a speedboat.

I don't love everything about GTA 6. The big action setpieces, while technically impressive, usually wind up feeling pretty samey: pull a big score, everything goes wrong, 100 guys show up, shoot all of them in the knees, then drive away, 100 cars show up, shoot all of them them in the tires (tires are a car's knees), escape. Rockstar missions are still Rockstar missions.

As with RDR2, these moments of front-page bombast contradict the fantasy of small-time outlaws struggling to get ahead, and GTA 6 goes full ridiculous with Fast and Furious-style mayhem. I'm not saying those sequences aren't entertaining, they just clash with the story of a couple of star-crossed crooks trying to save up enough money to get out of the game. And after you've shot your hundredth kneecap of the night, it gets a bit tiresome.

As for the story and characters? It's Rockstar, so some of it is genuinely good but a lot of it is exaggerated bluster. Lucia has some interactions with a family member that feel pretty real and there's a duo of rappers who are fun to spend time with, but I found the majority of the supporting characters either too grating or one-dimensional to care much about. Luckily, the writing and performances of Jason and Lucia make up for that. I enjoyed spending time with them. They had some raw moments that landed well. I felt feelings. I came to care about this couple.

If this is sounding too grown up, don't worry. There's a subplot about furries. A naked guy got into my car and took a sex toy out of his butt. There's a mission where you have to handle multiple dildos. The rideshare app's logo looks like a penis. All the actual penises also look like a penis, too. Rockstar is still Rockstar.

Now that I'm done with the main story, the real game can begin: just having fun in that big, beautiful sandbox. And I've got lots left to do: while I mentioned minigolf, there are actual, entire golf courses, too (this is Florida, remember).

I've done a bit of scuba diving for treasure but still have dozens of shipwrecks to discover. I don't find hunting much fun—hitscan sniper rifles aren't satisfying to use—but I sure like spotting new animals to check off my list, and there are over 200 of them to find. I've only caught one fish. I haven't done any drone races or stunt flying or base jumping or been to a shooting range. There are several in-game videogames I still have to play and a bunch of in-game TV shows to check out. I've somehow hardly gotten anything done in the two weeks I've been playing.

And this is deeply embarrassing, but I barely own any cars! I'm still mainly driving the muscle car I got very early in the game. It's not that there's not a lot to choose from—there are hundreds of autos to theft—it's that the handling and acceleration and physics of every car is different. That's great, obviously, but I quickly got used to driving a few cars and didn't want to have to learn the quirks of more vehicles while fleeing from the cops. Now that the story is behind me, though, it's finally time to start collecting.

I'm still trying to decide where I'd place GTA 6 among Rockstar's other games. RDR2 remains my favorite, followed by Red Dead Redemption, but do I like GTA 6 more than GTA 5? Ultimately, yeah, I just decided while writing this: I do. I like Jason and Lucia more than the three crooks from GTA 5, and maybe even more than I liked Niko Bellic in GTA 4. It's not entirely down to their personalities and performances, but also the systems Rockstar created to let me play as a couple, that make me feel like I had a co-op partner along for the ride.

I'm still trying to decide where I'd place GTA 6 among Rockstar's other games.

In a game like Skyrim where I can have followers, I almost always play solo. But in GTA 6, I found myself calling my partner to meet up almost every time I went out exploring. The game is better when they're together.

I wish we had some idea of when GTA 6 was coming to PC because after playing almost 100 hours on PS5, I'm desperate to get it on my desktop. I can't wait to see what modders can do with this thing (especially when they fix the weird cheat restrictions). As a PC gamer, I'm dying to aim at people's knees with my mouse instead of a thumbstick. And I'm especially curious to see what Rockstar has planned for an online mode (which they have said nothing about), and how FiveM, which Rockstar now owns, will tie into it. That big, beautiful world will only be better on PC where it belongs.

GTA 6 cheats are expected to be a huge part of the game. Saying you're going to use cheats in Grand Theft Auto is like saying water is wet—supplementing your cash, arsenal of weapons, or doing other fun stuff like turning off gravity is a core part of these games.

Unfortunately, this time you need to complete the main story—all 91 GTA 6 story missions —before you can access cheats and view their effects. After that, you'll have to complete the listed challenge to unlock each cheat command, though this does take into account what you've already done.

We loaded a save to test if cheat commands work earlier in the game and they don't. Our list also doesn't include some challenges, since we completed these while playing the game and so never got to see them.

First thing to note: if you use a cheat, you will not be able to save your game from that point on. That means you can't use cheats to progress through side missions or challenges, because with cheats on you'll have to quit your game without saving it.

Once unlocked, you can enter a cheat in GTA 6 if you:

Complete 50 skydives of base jumps from +300ft

Get 1st place in 10 races at Gellhorn Raceway, Thrillby Mud Club, and Boone Speedway

Win 20 bronze medals or better at shooting ranges

Win 25 silver medals or better at shooting ranges

Discover the Interstate Ambulance in the progress menu

Discover the MTL Pumper in the Progress menu

Clear 25 gang operations with your car partner

Discover Martha's Vamos in the Progress menu

Survive 6 minutes with a 6-star wanted level

Find all 24 collectible cards for the Vice City Flamingos

A factory worker experimented with a pressurized air system while on the job, and it resulted in a fatal injury.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The patient: A 35-year-old man in the Czech Republic

The symptoms: The man was injured while working in a factory. His co-workers learned he'd been hurt after he crawled from the ground floor to the first floor and shouted for help. He had severe abdominal pain and rectal bleeding, and he said he had been injured while conducting "a silly experiment" involving a pressurized air system. However, he did not describe exactly what had happened.

"He repeatedly stressed that the incident was his own fault," doctors later wrote in a report of his case.

What happened next: The man was flown by helicopter to a nearby hospital, but during the flight, he became unresponsive and showed signs of hemorrhagic shock — a type of shock caused by significant blood loss over a short period. Shock, broadly, is when organs and body tissues don't receive enough oxygen due to decreased blood flow; if untreated, it can lead to organ failure and death.

Medical attendants in the helicopter worked to revive the man, but he died before he could be admitted to the hospital. Because the fatal injury occurred at the man's workplace, the police ordered a medicolegal autopsy, which both identifies the cause of death and collects details for law enforcement agencies, as part of an inquest procedure.

The autopsy: The coroner examined the body and noted that the soft tissues of the man's face were swollen and abnormally distended from retained air. The man's anus and genital areas were similarly distended and densely coated with dried blood, with radial tears in the skin surrounding the anus.

Next, the coroner conducted an internal examination. The man's brain was swollen, and he had air bubbles in his brain and chest cavity. Blood had collected around his diaphragm (the large muscle that helps inflate and deflate the lungs). It had also accumulated in the wall between the heart chambers on the left side, in tubes leading to his lungs, and in the membranes covering his lungs and heart. Reservoirs of blood also pooled in the man's abdominal cavity, in the tube leading to his right kidney, and in his digestive organs.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

The man's heart was "shrunken and empty," according to the report.

The autopsy also revealed foreign objects stuck between loops of the man's small intestine. These included three pieces of a black rubber pipe stopper and scraps of a plastic bag. His rectum — the final straight portion of the large intestine — had detached violently from his anus. It was surrounded by blood and marked with a laceration that was nearly circular, indicating that an "explosive rectal injury" had triggered hemorrhagic shock and caused the man's death, the coroner concluded.

Further investigation: Additional evidence from the factory and rubber fragments in the man's small intestine provided the police with further insight into his injuries; additional clues came from his internet search history, including photos of himself that he'd submitted to an amateur sex website.

The police concluded that the man had been performing autoerotic anal stimulation while at work, using a rubber inflatable pipe stopper measuring 2 to 3 inches (50 to 70 millimeters) in diameter, and an air gun, a handheld device for directing powerful jets of compressed air.

They suggested that the man likely attached the expandable pipe stopper to the muzzle of the air gun, which was in turn connected to the factory's air distribution system by a long, high-pressure hose. He then covered the pipe stopper with a plastic bag, inserted it into his rectal cavity, and pressed the air gun's trigger, causing "an unexpected abrupt inflation and explosive bursting of the pipe stopper within his rectum," the doctors wrote in the case report.

What makes the case unique: This case is the first recorded example of a person dying from a "rectal explosion during self-gratification," the doctors wrote. Piecing together the circumstances leading up to the man's injury was important for the hospital's doctors and law enforcement to understand how the fatality likely occurred, the authors said.

When performed responsibly and consensually, rectal insertion of foreign bodies typically does not cause significant injury, the authors added. However, "the introduction of some objects into the rectum might have unpredictable and even fatal effects."

For more intriguing medical cases, check out our Diagnostic Dilemma archives.

This article is for informational purposes only and is not meant to offer medical advice.

Hejna, P., Zátopková, L., & Janík, M. (2020). Rectal explosion: A strange case of autoerotic death. International Journal of Legal Medicine. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00414-020-02344-7

Funny, sad, euphoric… GTA 6 is the most entertaining and emotionally engaging open world I’ve played. Rockstar has taken the sandbox freedom of Grand Theft Auto and the environmental storytelling of Red Dead Redemption 2 and made something that feels lived-in. The characters, humour, and systems are all wonderfully written, and the attention to detail makes Leonida a place I want to stay in long after I’d finished the story. The set pieces rival Hollywood, but I'll remember the small, unplanned moments.

An extraordinarily detailed, living open world

Jason and Lucia are brilliant protagonists

Hilarious, unpredictable emergent gameplay

Superb environmental storytelling and art direction

Why you can trust Creative Bloq Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test.

In brief: 5/5. Grand Theft Auto VI (reviewed on PS5, out 19 November) is the most convincing open world I’ve played.

I laughed out loud multiple times within minutes of starting Grand Theft Auto VI. Not a chuckle or a smirk, but proper laughs, grinning ear to ear, as a particularly large resident of Leonida giggled, ran, stumbled, staggered and tripped over a railing into the river below. It was ridiculous and completely unexpected, and I loved it.

We've waited 13 years for GTA VI and from the opening credits, Rockstar has crafted a hyperreal but intensely personal world where every corner of Leonida and Vice City offers a surprise. I've been playing for three weeks, finished the story, seen some endings, and I'm still playing to find out what random secrets Leonida has left to share. Much of it has nothing to do with the fate of Lucia and Jason, GTA VI's modern-day Bonnie and Clyde. (Read our GTA VI coverage for more on the game.)

Driving around, you'll spot Just Stop Oil-style protests blocking traffic, teenagers dropping rocks onto motorway cars, or posters and flyers that lead to mysteries and new characters to call from your iFruit phone's contacts list. These aren't side quests in the traditional sense, with a marker on your map and a list to tick off; they're connections to random people, and the sense that this world exists beyond the screen.

Those teenagers dropping rocks? I detoured to teach them a lesson. Later, I stopped for someone posting for social media while balancing on a bridge, and failed to save him when he fell, and I actually felt bad. I pulled over for some teens daring each other to jump from a bridge into a river, decided to show them how it was done, and while I was swimming, they stole my car.

It's not risk and reward; it's just life in Leonida. It's incredibly fun.

The scale of GTA VI is incredible, but not in the usual sense of a vast map to cross. It's the depth and detail that gets me: the branding, signage, store shelves of snacks and comic books that can be read, snatches of conversations from passersby muttering about their lives or something they heard on the radio, the same thing I heard on the radio. Most buildings can be broken into and explored, and I've spent far too long sneaking into warehouses that have no obvious reason to exist beyond making the world feel authentic and the possibility that something of value could be snaffled away inside.

Sign up to Creative Bloq's daily newsletter, which brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of art, design and technology.

Shops, bars and clubs are lovingly detailed, and once inside you're free to toy with the world. Buy something, drink something for a stat bonus, steal something, change your clothes, or earwig and people watch. Sometimes you'll need to change outfits, because it throws off the cops chasing you; sometimes just because you feel you should wear beach clothes on the beach, because I'm completely hooked into this world.

The geography is considered too. Vice City is a maze of overpasses and winding spaghetti motorway junctions; the city itself is a muddle of back alleys, malls, and beachfront hotels, while the roads out in the country are simpler and more relaxed; the swamps need care to navigate; the sandy, wooded isles of the north are a stolen boat. Beaches, swamps, forests and distinct neighbourhoods all have their own character, and you feel it: stressed in Vice City, calm and playful up north, the mullet of map design, if you will. Even the residents and police behave differently depending on where you are.

Early on, Jason and Lucia visit a rich, enclaved community filled with jewellery shops, polished pavements and high-fashion stores practically demanding to be robbed. A policeman on a bicycle stops them and warns them that their kind isn't welcome. I pushed my luck, choosing confrontational dialogue options, refused to obey, and he called in backup from other pedal-bike cops who made it clear our kind wasn't welcome. I returned at night and stole everything, and it felt so good.

Giving you an emotional reason to do things is one of GTA VI's biggest successes. You start to understand the people who live here, the divisions between communities and the little injustices that make you want to cause trouble.

There's always something happening, too. An armoured car is robbed, so I follow it to the thieves' hideout and steal everything. A farm sign says 'pilot wanted', so I drop in and end up in a whole side story about meth-strawberries that eventually riffs on a Marvel character I never expected. Leonida's residents are 'Karens on crack', too. Scrape someone's car, and they'll chase you down; look at someone too long, and they'll demand a fight; drive down a motorway, and hyped up teen will lean out of their car to challenge you to a race. Once I planned a bank heist, only to find a random gang shooting the place up, and I got caught in the melee. It's layer upon layer of random, living events, and even on a mission, it's easy to get sidetracked as gunshots ring out.

GTA VI rewards your downtime too; it wants you to simply enjoy the place and the moment because conversations eavesdropped on in a bar are hilarious but also tease secrets about the world, whether residents are complaining about the weather or arguing over culture-war nonsense raised by the State's shock jock, who is furious about that weekend's Manatees football result and the demise of 'mansculinity'. Some can be engaged with and will share random but useful news about Leonida.

There's no Ubisoft-style checklist here. Stunts, hidden collectable cards (which you can sell in-game), fishing challenges and sporting events are there if you want them, but the world grows as you explore, meet people and build up your contacts list. You just exist in Leonida and enjoy exploring, competing and completing things.

The weather is a big part of that experience, because it looks beautiful – golden morning sunlight cuts through thick mist over a wildflower meadow with realism, dramatic storm clouds and dense golden fog engulf a city skyline, obscuring buildings and bridges in an atmospheric haze.

But weather also affects how you engage with the world. Days feel long enough to play in, different things happen at different times, and the weather is dramatic and distinct. That hazy mist can obscure your visibility, while hard rain can limit distance and disrupt sound, something used to dramatic effect in a nighttime kidnapping rescue where large halogen lights pierced the rain and mist, creating drama but affecting line of sight in some spaces.

Likewise, a plane handles differently in wind, rain and cloud, as the controls judder and inputs feel less responsive. Flying through a storm, with lightning sparking and rolling across the horizon, gives you a real sense of place and moment but also puts you slightly on edge.

Jason and Lucia's relationship really surprised me in GTA VI, and it's one area where Rockstar picks up where Red Dead Redemption 2 left off. Both are well-rounded protagonists with motivations and shared dreams that you help build. Lucia is alive and sprightly, Jason is dour and determined, and how their connection develops, or doesn't, becomes a game of its own.

A subtle romance and empathy system is at play. How much time the pair spend together, the conversations you choose, the dates, time at home (yes, you can make love in the shower, on the sofa, in the kitchen and, well, all sorts of places) and even how and when you plan and commit crimes all feed into how their relationship develops, and it can affect how their story ends.

What you do on a job matters too. Kill lots of people, and you get a different criminal rating than if you spare lives, and the duo seem to have a healthier relationship if you play to control a room with threats or shoot to injure rather than murder. I wanted a loving crime couple, so almost without meaning to, I started shooting people in the legs and arms to make them fall or drop their guns instead of headshotting everyone in a room. I wanted my Lucia to like my Jason.

Likewise, when Jason went undercover as 'the poolboy' for a saucy film shoot, I held back on how far I took things. Lucia was getting madder in my ear as Jason applied lotion to an actress, and when given the choice to go all in, as it were, I pulled out, as they say, as it were, because I wanted Lucia to still like Jason. I still don't know how far you can take that mission, but this is Rockstar, so I imagine it's all the way (and that's what she said).

Few games get that emotional connection right. It doesn't come only from good writing and characterisation, but from all the little conversations, actions, reactions and animated moments when they meet up or succeed. You'd have a heart of stone to go out of your way to ruin their romance, because you can. You monster.

Controlling when and how they meet up is part of GTA V's character-switching development. Moving between them is nearly instantaneous: the camera pulls out to a global view, zooms back down, and you can message the other to hook up or tell them to meet you somewhere. And you do get committed: when I occasionally Irish-goodbye'd Jason, I felt the need to call him and check up.

The central narrative picks up what worked in Red Dead Redemption 2, splitting the story into chapters that each introduce a new gang or cast and a grand setup to plan towards. The structure gives you plenty to play with, and the story spans more years as the couple bounces from backwater crimes to epic, militarised heists. These feed into cinematic tentpole moments that draw on everything from the later Fast and Furious movies to Assault on Precinct 13, with even a little nod to Die Hard as Lucia sparks a lighter in an air vent, laughs and paraphrases the classic line, "Come out to the coast, we'll get together, have a few laughs."

It's also where Rockstar's love of a good heist movie really shines. Some of the bigger set pieces have the clockwork precision of an Edgar Wright film, with different characters, objectives and moving parts all working towards one carefully choreographed finale. The editing is part of the fun: the action cuts between Jason and Lucia as they tackle their separate jobs, each sequence dovetailing with the next as the plan unfolds, the clock ticks down, and the stakes rise.

The grand finales of each chapter are proper spectacles that never play out the same way and deliver 'cinema'. You might be flying gunships over a stormy ocean, or swapping between Jason and Lucia as they complete different parts of a larger plan. Jason races to a rooftop to stop mobster reinforcements while Lucia hacks a vault, and you're jumping between the two as the action cuts back and forth, the tempo building with each switch. One moment you're holding off a gang; the next, you're working through the other side of the operation, and it all clicks together like clockwork. It's a wonderfully cinematic way to make character switching part of the action, not just a convenient way to get around the map.

Around these set pieces that take time to build are lower-key missions, some tailored to each character, and this is where Rockstar earns its rewards. The satire of modern America, social media, celebrity culture and consumerism that we love about GTA is here in abundance. A favourite is a storyline in which Lucia becomes embroiled in a bored-housewives vape cult that's like Goop meets Elizabeth Holmes.

Then there are the random encounters that make Leonida feel active, and never run how you think. An elderly woman screaming for help on a back road took me to her farmhouse, where I expected a robbery or a rescue. Instead, a client had 'died' in a bondage orgy gone wrong, and I needed to dispose of the body in a river. Even that didn't end as I expected.

Even 40-plus hours into the main story, Rockstar finds new ways to surprise me. It introduces a vault-hacking mini-game that uses haptics and controller prompts for one bank job, then drops in a drug-dog sidekick for a single mission. Ideas are picked up, enjoyed and dropped before they go stale. GTA VI has so many that it never has to hang around with one for long.

Shooting and weapon handling are superb, and each gun feels distinct. The cover system and enemy AI respond nicely even in busy rooms, and stealth is reliable and effective. While the big set-piece story missions can feel a little restrictive and scripted because they need to reach the cinematic heights Rockstar is aiming for, anything can happen outside them.

A bank heist, for example, needs proper planning. Park a getaway car, choose the right vehicle, pick the rear door lock, hack the cameras, wear a disguise, and don't overstay your welcome. The world is so well designed and systematised that everything feels connected. Next time, go in through the front door, or steal a truck and pull an ATM from the wall. Heists in backwater towns are easier because there are fewer police around. And nothing plays out quite as you expect; every bank is unique, and after two seamless jobs I go for a third and it all goes wrong – an unexpected teller wanders into the office for a coffee, an alarm is tripped, and before I realise it, I'm shooting my way out, bags shouldered, and looking for a new car to steal… the best-laid plans are shot.

The police react to all this more deeply than in previous GTAs. There's no longer just a star rating and a zone to escape, but how you escape matters. Swap cars and clothes, and they'll lose you, because they're looking for your description, not you, me, the player. All the old tricks are still here, from roadblocks and air support to increasingly aggressive police AI, but you have new ways to shake them off beyond just driving fast.

It ties into car ownership too, another Red Dead Redemption 2 influence. You can't carry everything, so it's worth stowing a change of clothes and weapons in your car. Carrying a gun openly gets the police involved, but some Vice City passers-by will also decide to take you out as well.

Driving feels familiar from GTA V, but with enough nuance to feel like an evolution, as cars have different weights and handling, and each one reacts differently through the DualSense triggers: sports cars resist less than family saloons when you pull to accelerate. Boats, bikes, planes and helicopters all work as you'd expect, but even here there are subtle shifts in how responsive each can be – one helicopter I stole was uncontrollable and spun into the swamp.

Character models, facial animation, skin, hair, and clothing all deliver the hyperrealism I expected from a new GTA, though they're still larger-than-life caricatures built to feel relatable rather than photorealistic.

Animation, including the transitions between gameplay and cutscenes, is where GTA VI takes its biggest strides. Lucia and Jason are wonderfully handled, whether it's the little snuggles and embraces or the way they hold up a bank and play off one another, but the breadth of animation across GTA VI is what impresses. Every Leonida resident feels uniquely animated, and it's fun just to people-watch. Early on, a drunk girl follows Jason around a bar and is authentically annoying, and the nightlife feels realistically overwhelming. Bar bands are animated to sell their next song, and even the wildlife has moments: I watched a white-tailed doe and buck nuzzle each other lovingly and naturally through Jason's rifle scope. It was cute enough to make me take a breath, but Jason needs more money, so the shot rang out and the wildlife scattered.

Leonida has a recognisable visual identity, bold and vibrant, with every corner full of quirks, from the deep forests of the north to the out-of-town mall and rows of copy-and-paste suburban houses. Fictional adverts, billboards, shops, signage, and TV build the world, as if you see an ad for a beer or car, and you can buy it (or steal it). Beyond signage, graffiti walls, sculptures, exhibits, and more invite you to linger and just take in the world.

It also feels like a realistic evolution of the 1980s Vice City I knew and loved, a city with a history inside a broader world, with references to Liberty City aplenty, from car number plates to Jason and Lucia's accents. It's somewhere to wallow, whether you're having a cocktail under palm trees swaying in a breeze or tearing up Vice City in a neon-lit supercar while crypto bros trade and wannabe rappers parade.

It's a wonder this all runs on a base PS5. I remember the mess of equally ambitious games like Cyberpunk 2077 at launch, but GTA VI is in a different league. The frame rate is locked at 30fps, and it's fine: stable, with little slowdown or stutter, and controls and handling feel spot on. There's occasional soft pop-in, but few visual compromises or trip-ups. You can feel the work that's gone into making everything run smoothly, and GTA 6 is polished to perfection.

I'm really only scratching the surface. Familiar street races, bank heists, and chilled fishing and hunting trips are joined by crypto rug pulls, golf tournaments, and deep-sea treasure hunts. Or I just drive, hunt a swamp thing, stop to solve a mystery from a local ad, or relax with a game of pool and a Patriot beer. You can take on the State's sports and races, go sailing, or listen to 80s FM hits, the biggest dance tracks, or to the MAGA-inspired Richard Bastion Show – "more volume than logic" – who's mad about everything.

This game has video games inside it that feel more complete than some real games I've played, from the top-down sci-fi shooter Time Jackers: Rewind to a lightgun score-chasing bar game Bang For Your Buck. And in typical Rockstar fashion, they all have a satirical edge, like the indie auteur game Tenebrae Lux, which pokes fun at the po-faced walking sims that were all the rage: it's black-and-white, minimal, and filled with overwritten prose like a Taylor Swift song about metaphors.

GTA VI is a world that exists beyond its main story, where everything feeds into and off each other. It's the best world-building I've experienced in a game in years, partly because its systems all work in a coherent, purposeful and layered way, but also because it's not afraid to be weird, whether that's discovering the dumpster lawyer, becoming a frog, slobbing on the sofa and watching an episode of Whose Dick's Whose, or finding an influencer in the boot of a stolen car who wants to be kidnapped for clout.

There are minor restrictions, mainly when the big cinematic missions take over and funnel you down a more scripted path, but for good reason, and the 30fps cap won't suit everyone (yet it's really not an issue). But in a game that otherwise gives you this much freedom, they're the exception.

13 years? The wait has been worthwhile. I still set off with a plan, get distracted by something ridiculous at the side of the road, and lose another hour to a game I thought I'd finished. I laughed within minutes of starting, and I laugh every time I play. I've also been stressed, revolted, astonished, baffled, heartbroken and euphoric. I've run the full gamut of emotions, and I still do each time I return to Vice City.

Yesterday, the Trump administration extended the reach of its existing export controls on high-end AI accelerator chips, namely, but not limited to, Nvidia's Blackwell lineup. The updated regulation now requires licenses for renting those chips in large quantities to the entirety of America's D:5 countries list (nations embargoed from arms sales). As expected, the news landed in Beijing like a lead dragon, and its Ministry of Commerce states that China "will take countermeasures to firmly safeguard national sovereignty, security, and development interests."

The bold move taken by the U.S. arrives at a peculiar time, as President Trump is currently visiting the nation for the APEC summit in Shenzhen. Trump is scheduled to meet President Xi Jinping on Thursday, Nov. 19, a tête-a-tête that's bound to be interesting. Both nations were recently embroiled in a bitter trade war, with ever-mounting tariffs and restrictions on both sides until a temporary truce was called in Oct. 2025. Only some restrictions were lifted, though; for example, Chinese semiconductors still face a 50% tariff when imported stateside.

A potential restart of tariff-slapping would all but guarantee an even larger amount of turmoil in U.S. stock markets. Those seas are already choppy enough thanks to Nvidia ex-CEO Jensen Huang's romantic involvement with purported Chinese spy Alice Huang — along with mounting suspicions that the soulmates may have connived to siphon billions' worth of Blackwell chips from her Singaporean outfit Megaspeed onto Chinese AI laboratories.

Nvidia cut off about half of its Asian buyers last July, seemingly in the purview of the export controls, and told data center operators that over 50% of their business must come from non-Chinese companies. Meanwhile, both Malaysia and Singapore have intensified their scrutiny of AI hardware shipments.

China's countermeasures ammo is as of yet unspecified. The nation had restricted the sale of gallium, germanium, and antimony to the U.S. previously, and the truce shelved that bullet until Nov. 2027. Beijing may well choose to simply not renew that agreement when that day comes. Although analysts believe that the nations will be cordial enough during this summit, Trump's perceived provocation may bring China's proverbial nuclear option of restricting rare earth exports back to the loading bay.

The truce on that particular matter only has a few weeks left, expiring on Jan. 10, 2027. Likewise, super-hard materials and high-density lithium batteries, crucial for the newest generations of EVs, solar power storage, and battery installations, all have white flags that will come down early next year. Analysts also expect that Chinese firms and their government will continue to heavily invest in domestic chip production, namely, but not only, by Huawei.

Broadly speaking, the U.S.' updated chip control regulation means that Chinese firms cannot sidestep the existing control on chip sales by renting them instead, closing one of the main existing loopholes around the export restrictions. Additionally, selling chips to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, or Brazil now also requires a license, as the U.S. Department of Commerce suspects that companies in these nations import Blackwell cards to sell to China.

Exclusive: Germ DM Is a Signal Alternative That’s Now on Android

📅 Nov 18, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

Tessa Brown is visibly excited to talk to me about Germ DM, her secure messaging platform. It’s now available on Android, a major expansion for the small startup. Her eyes light up as she explains how her ambitious, three-person team—including an ex-Apple engineer who worked on iMessage—could pull off this platform expansion.

“It's essential to be able to talk to everybody, and that's really what this Android launch unlocks for us,” she says. Brown was previously a lecturer at Stanford University, and her cofounder, Mark Xue, worked on iMessage’s privacy provisions. The duo first launched the iOS app for Germ in 2023.

The platform expansion makes it easier to recommend Germ as an interesting alternative to Signal, especially for early adopters curious about trying new ways to message others and connect with the world.

My favorite aspect about Germ is that the platform doesn’t nudge you to attach a phone number. “Germ is a multi-identity messenger,” Brown says. “The way walled gardens are constructed means that every time you log into an app you get one identity that the app owns.” On Germ, it’s not about creating a permanent handle that you give to everyone; multiplicity is central to this messenger’s pitch.

Tessa Brown and Mark Xue, cofounders of Germ Network.

The app revolves around “burner cards.” Each card works like a separate phone line built into the app. Instead of a dedicated number or a public handle, you can share these Germ cards in two ways: a QR code or a direct link. You can scan QR codes inside the app if meeting someone in person. For digital connections, you can generate a custom link tied to the card, from just one to 100.

After downloading the app, you create these cards by tapping on the green plus button under the Me tab. Choose the name, pronouns, and photo you want to use for that card. Cards associated with your Germ account are not mutually discoverable, and who you connect with on each card is private. As the name suggests, if you delete these “burners” at any time, the connections associated with that card will no longer be able to contact you, and those chats will be removed from your device.

The Germ network runs on Messaging Layer Security, built by the Internet Engineering Task Force as an end-to-end encryption standard. When you are exchanging those “burner cards,” you are actually exchanging cryptographic keys with your new contacts. However, Germ has not undergone a third-party audit, though Brown is open to doing so in the future.

“People want to share different parts of themselves with different people,” Brown says. “Queer folks get Germ immediately; it's not just queer people. It's also people who are gig workers and creatives that have multiple jobs.” Germ is built to share with people in different parts of your life and let them contact you in a central hub through distinct messaging channels.

Xue is serious about the work Germ put into building a secure platform, including addressing the looming issue of quantum computing. Essentially, security experts worry that super-powerful computers could break encryption protections and reveal previously private messages. Developers at large messaging platforms, like iMessage and Signal, have built protections against these quantum concerns. “What we've accomplished as a small team is we've reached the same level of security,” he says. Germ publicly laid out how the platform claims to be “quantum secure.”

Germ’s most recent success came from its integration with Bluesky. Since that social media platform is built on the Authenticated Transfer Protocol, Bluesky users can connect their existing handles to Germ and display it as a messaging button in their profile. This lets friends on the platform easily send you encrypted texts. While many users enjoy that platform-specific integration, Germ’s expansion to Android is a fresh opportunity to meet a new user base.

Brown already has her sights set on Germ’s next move: group chats.

“We’ve worked together this whole time over the belief that the future of communication is in private chats,” she says. For now, the platform supports one-on-one conversations, but the team is ready to build support for larger, group threads.

It might be hard to convince your group chat to switch to a new app, but flashing a QR code to a stranger you just met to continue a conversation could actually work.

UBI Breeds Dependence and Restricts Opportunity

📅 Nov 18, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

The new Democratic Congress should walk away from the destructive path of this policy.

Democrats seized control of Congress, in part by focusing on affordability and the economy. An AP-NORC survey conducted just before the election found that both were ranked top issues for registered voters, outpacing the next most important issue, health care, by about 15 percentage points.

The new Democratic Congress will presumably pursue policies that are advertised as ways to reduce the cost of living. One idea they should reject is universal basic income (UBI). Leftists have long pushed for UBI, and the idea is gaining stream among tech leaders. It’s a policy that would backfire by reigniting inflation and ultimately harming those it attempts to help.

GTA VI Is the Most Anticipated Video Game in Human History. It Lives Up to the Hype.

📅 Nov 18, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

There are moments in GTA 6 that’ll have you levitating off your sofa. Unprecedented in its scope and production, it was created by a team of almost 5,000 developers over nearly 10 years. Its budget is rumored to rival the construction of Dubai’s Burj Khalifa skyscraper; its first trailer set records with 93 million views in a day. Every social media brand account, from the White House to BMW, has jumped on the hype, while economists predict a national sick day as millions play hooky to game. When you do, you see the time, talent and flair on the screen. But, at its heart, Grand Theft Auto VI follows in series tradition: an epic American crime story, set in a stunning parody of the US that riffs on film, music, politics, style and satire.

Fronting the first franchise entry in more than 13 years are Jason and Lucia. Developer Rockstar attempted a multi-character arc in Grand Theft Auto V, but those three leads learned to loathe one another. Instead, VI tackles love, a game design challenge most developers have sworn off with good reason. Not a parent/child relationship like The Last of Us or God of War, but a mature, romantic, adult one. You can call or text each other at pretty much any point—to do missions together, commit robberies, explore, meditate, work out, fly, or just to coexist under the Vice City sunshine.

This isn’t some kind of ChatGPT fantasy to indulge in. Neither Jason or Lucia exists at your beck and call as some kind of hyper-realistic plaything. You have a role in their relationship, both in the way they speak to each other and where the story takes them. You can cruise down the Vice City waterfront together in your souped-up '70s muscle wagon with one of you driving, the other scrolling through your Snapmatic feed (the in-game social media channel), before grabbing a drink and carving up the sidewalk with an assault rifle five minutes later. You just don’t get these detours in Call of Duty.

More than a car: in GTA VI, your vehicle is a mobile base of operations to stash your guns, fits, money and drugs.

It’s a different pace from previous Grand Theft Autos too. Rockstar changed its dynamics with 2018’s Red Dead Redemption 2—a more thoughtful take on the outlaw tale that added friction to the action and a conscience to the narrative. For a developer that once experienced the spotlight of US Congress during 2005’s infamous “Hot Coffee" controversy (when a sexually explicit mini-game meant as an inside joke between developers was figured out by savvy users), this kind of nuance was revelatory. With VI, Rockstar takes Red Dead 2’s ethos and applies it to a modern city with 1,000 x the population. The result is staggering, but still an absolute blast to play. That is to say, the greatest hits of GTA—driving cars, shooting guns, and stealing money, drugs and more (all to spend on a better Beretta, G-Wagon replica, and impeccably modeled Air Jordan dupes)—but with added depth to how you play. Weapon slots are finite; you can no longer run amok with an entire arsenal stashed in your jacket pocket. Money is vulnerable; get killed or caught with cash in your possession, and you’ll lose it. And if you jack a car that’s fitted with a tracker, the police will find you quickly.

Should you get into a bust-up with the law after a jewelry store smash-and-grab gone wrong, the game’s action is frenetic. Roads are much narrower, traffic is denser, and you can’t see police on your minimap. That $40,000 in cash sitting on the back seat had better be worth the hassle. As such, the game supports your decision to play chaotically, but truly immerses you in playing methodically. Jason and Lucia each have a “criminal profile”—be unnecessarily violent and you’ll get a “psycho” rating—that adds replayability and roleplay. Still, I had the most fun when planning missions: using a silenced pistol, shooting to maim not kill, and wiping security footage to leave no trace. It’s the closest GTA has honed in on the art of crime. The feds will surround the store you’re robbing. “Come out right now with your hands above your head!” Do things right, and you’ll have prepped your partner with a getaway car out back. You’ll leave the scene anonymously as backup blares past you on the other side of the road.

Every club, pub and dingy dive bar in GTA 6’s Leonida has a distinct vibe—from the music to the decor to the sweaty Floridians inside.

The game kicks off with an electrifying setup accompanied by an original song from composers Justice. It perfectly sets the tone: VI has the '80s flamboyance of Vice City made new and fresh. It takes its opening hours steadily, sending you on odd jobs to make a little money here and there. Gradually—then suddenly—you’re thrust into the most high-octane campaign in Grand Theft Auto history. Tense hospital escapes, daring bank heists, cross-country chases, and more. Its set pieces are balls-to-the-wall bravado, rivaling what you’d see in Nolan’s The Odyssey or Villeneuve’s Dune, upping in intensity through its chapters. Tonally, it’s the most “of the now" Grand Theft Auto game yet, as your two in-love criminals race to find a better life in an unfair world. No previous GTA has given you a savings account—it’s like playing the millennial curse. The only dings are some pacing in the game’s second chapter as the game wrestles with its story while still introducing mechanics. Think of it as VI’s version of RDR2’s Guarma, albeit with bargain bin stores and grimy strip malls instead of exotic Caribbean fauna.

And then to Leonida, with which Rockstar has created the most technically and artistically impressive game world ever made. The pre-release trailers promised beaches bustling with vacationers and nightclubs packed with dancers. That is the reality. From sea to sand to sky, the world is alive. Vice City alone could be an entire game in its own right, complete with distinct districts, an explorable international airport, and more. Yet, Rockstar spoils us with a massive expanse of varied towns, high-class beach resorts, lush green national parks, murky swamplands and sun-kissed island keys. All packed with people that range from useful, to funny, to completely unsavory (shout-out to the old woman who took one look at my Jason and said “I’mma take my teeth out and suck the skin off that dick”). The density and fidelity of it all often stretches the limits of even Sony’s PlayStation 5 Pro. Frame rate dips don’t spoil gameplay, but the slowdown is noticeable when you’ve punted a couple of grenades into passing cars to set off multiple explosions at once.

NPCs don’t just feel like backdrop mannequins anymore, but real people with an incredible range of faces, body types and outfits.

Every frame a photograph. Stop anywhere in GTA 6, and you’ll likely find something enticing to see, hear or interact with.

As with Red Dead Redemption 2, the most impressive of the game’s many achievements is how everything seems to live on without you. All it took to make this world was Rockstar founding an entire studio to work solely on Leonida’s population. I’ve seen a woman throw herself out of a cop car window as I scooted along Ocean Beach, and car thieves burst through the glass windows of a car dealership while the alarms howl. I saw a furry taken down by armed police, staged perfectly with a helicopter spotlight. During one 3am wander through the rough neighborhood of Crosstown, a man approached me to warn me of the local gang and tells me they have a nearby base. I accidentally tapped the button that brings up your in-game phone. “Ohhhh! You don’t just believe what I say” the man says, responding to my actions. “You do your own research!” In more than 70 hours of play, I have seen only one moment of repetition.

There is so much more besides. A cast of interesting, funny and believable characters; off-the-beaten-path secrets that can lead to side quests both big and small; perhaps the best radio track list of any GTA spanning from Travis Scott to Lana Del Rey; podcast episodes; golf to play; 'gators to hunt; dozens of supercars to steal and customize; weapons that feel punchy and satisfying; multiple racing series; a litany of actually interesting shops and bars and clubs to explore and buy things in. I’ve seen brilliant horror vignettes, startling science fiction, and laugh-out-loud comedy just by exploring. Rockstar has created a world that rewards you for spending time in it. Expect to spend 100 hours if you want to see everything.

As you’ll likely have seen and heard—in everything from Miami Heat takeovers, to Netflix launches, to Selfridges pop-ups—that this is the most-wanted entertainment property in the world. In a way, all it had to be was Grand Theft Auto V: The Second. But, on the largest and most scrutinized stage imaginable, Rockstar takes creative risks with its story, protagonists, and mechanics, and makes big leaps in what games can be. It’s unlikely other developers will catch up soon. In 2002, Grand Theft Auto: Vice City reshaped and refashioned pop culture to give us a playable version of a place and a time we already knew. A quarter of a century later, VI shows Rockstar at the peak of entertainment in its very own right.

China dominates battery graphite, but this startup could break the monopoly

📅 Nov 18, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

Electric vehicle sales in the U.S. may have leveled off, but the market for batteries inside them isn’t slowing down, quintupling in the last five years. Many of those are made in the U.S., but they’re largely dependent on China for key ingredients, including graphite.

Graphite is a key ingredient in lithium-ion batteries, where it forms the anode, the part that stores the battery’s charge. Chinese companies control about three-quarters of the graphite anode supply chain and 97% of synthetic (human-made) graphite anode production, according to Benchmark Mineral Intelligence. One five-year-old startup, Molten Industries, is working to break that dominance.

Molten Industries has started operating a demonstration plant in Oakland meant to prove the technology works, the company exclusively told TechCrunch. The plant is will pave the way for U.S.-made graphite to win a share of the market.

“The new plant will be producing graphite that’s at cost parity with China plus tariffs,” Caleb Boyd, co-founder and CTO of Molten Industries, told TechCrunch. In other words, once U.S. import taxes are added to Chinese graphite, Molten’s price would match it. He said future plants should match China’s cost even without tariffs, which he called a built-in advantage of the technology.

Molten’s Oakland plant will make about 300 metric tons of graphite annually, which is enough for 300 megawatt-hours of batteries. That’s enough for about 4,300 EVs. The bulk of the output will go to undisclosed customers that are testing it in their battery cells.

The next facility, which Molten has yet to announce, will take the same template used in the Oakland plant and replicate it several times over, said Boyd.

The startup’s technology began in a Silicon Valley garage. It uses electrical resistive heating, which passes electricity through a material to heat it, to split methane (the main ingredient in natural gas) into pure carbon and hydrogen. “You can think of it almost like a massive toaster,” Boyd said. The company says the system uses three times less electricity than existing methods, and it runs on natural gas, which is cheap and plentiful in the U.S.

“We think it’s very hard to compete with China if you’re just copying their processes and trying to compete on cost,” said Kevin Bush, who co-founded Molten Industries with Boyd and is the company’s CEO. “So we are using a resource in the United States that’s abundant in natural gas, and we’ve brought some innovation to actually be able to drive down the cost of graphite production globally.”

Here’s how the chemistry works: When methane (CH4) is heated without oxygen, each molecule breaks into one carbon atom and four hydrogen atoms. The hydrogen atoms pair up into hydrogen gas (H2), which Molten sells at market prices to a customer next door. The carbon is then processed to meet battery makers’ requirements.

The basic idea of using heat to separate methane has been around for over a century, but early attempts to commercialize it ran into trouble. Carbon built up and clogged the reactor, and Boyd said no company before Molten had been able to produce high-quality graphite this way.

Solving that problem changed the company’s direction. Boyd and Bush — both materials science PhDs from Stanford — originally set out to make clean hydrogen from natural gas. Most hydrogen today comes from steam reforming, a cheap but polluting process. The two wanted to reap the benefits of a low-cost feedstock like natural gas without the pollution, and they expected to sell the leftover carbon as a byproduct.

But as they experimented with ways to keep the reactor clean, “we actually started making this really high quality graphite,” Boyd said, which “changed the entire economics of what we were doing.” Molten went from a hydrogen company that happened to sell graphite to a battery-grade graphite company that happens to sell hydrogen.

The company says both businesses could bring in billions of dollars. If Molten supplied the entire U.S. battery market, it could also provide about a third of the hydrogen used in the country, the company claims. Other uses for high-quality graphite, like thermal batteries that store energy as heat, could expand both markets further.

The new factory, Boyd said, “is really a milestone, not just for the company, we think, but globally.”

Tim De Chant is a senior climate reporter at TechCrunch. He has written for a wide range of publications, including Wired magazine, the Chicago Tribune, Ars Technica, The Wire China, and NOVA Next, where he was founding editor.

De Chant is also a lecturer in MIT’s Graduate Program in Science Writing, and he was awarded a Knight Science Journalism Fellowship at MIT in 2018, during which time he studied climate technologies and explored new business models for journalism.
