Affairs, geopolitics, and the global AI race. Plus a whole lot of money.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Nvidia rose from a niche gaming hardware company with an unofficial motto of "Our company is thirty days from going out of business” to becoming the world’s most valuable company by market capitalization in 2024, and co-founder and chief executive Jensen Huang was the man behind its meteoric rise.

He planned and founded the company in 1993 alongside Chris Malachowsky and Curtis Priem while sitting inside a Denny’s diner in the Silicon Valley area. After more than 30 years, Nvidia had thousands of employees, a global footprint, and a name that people equated to AI chips.

All this came crumbling down for the billionaire founder in a matter of weeks, but the cracks started long before the first accusation. Let’s go back and see how it all began. This is an ongoing saga, so we have listed stories related to the scandal below, which we will update as events unfold.

Jensen resigned from Nvidia on November 12, after two weeks of news reports accusing him of multiple affairs, one with an alleged Chinese spy and another with his own subordinate. This is significant for Nvidia, which has had a single CEO since its inception. Huang was the face of the company, and many of its employees, shareholders, partners, and fans still support him despite the circumstances of his departure. He steered Nvidia into the giant that it is today by having the vision to develop CUDA nearly 20 years before ChatGPT made AI accessible to the average user and buying companies that helped it scale deployments to hundreds of thousands of AI GPUs.

By 2022, ChatGPT’s arrival and subsequent boom set the AI race in motion, with tech giants and AI startups buying up as many GPUs as they could get their hands on. The increased demand for Nvidia’s products caused it to break the trillion-dollar mark in less than a year after the release of OpenAI’s LLM. As the largest individual shareholders of the company, Huang and his wife, Lori, became some of the wealthiest people in the world.

The billionaire founder hasn't always gloated about his position. He once said in a podcast that if he could turn back time, he wouldn’t have founded Nvidia at all, and also cringed at the praises that the Caltech Board of Trustees chairperson heaped on him before he gave the 2024 keynote speech at the institute’s commencement exercises. He has frequently cited his history working as a “Dishwasher, Busboy, Waiter” at Denny’s, noting it under his experience on his LinkedIn page. More than that, people have seen Jensen go where other celebrity CEOs are rarely seen — enjoying street food in Vietnam, dining at a local fried chicken joint in Korea, and even dragging along 35 of Taiwan’s semiconductor CEOs to a restaurant in Taipei.

But even as he’s building his “Man of the People” persona, his position as the head of arguably the most important chipmaker in the AI industry meant that he was also gaining influence in business and governance. Industry leaders noticed the power that Nvidia held over those who want GPUs to train their AI models, with some of his fellow billionaires begging him over dinner to sell them GPUs. Just weeks into President Donald Trump’s second term, Jensen Huang was meeting with him at the White House, discussing AI policy and hardware export controls — something the Biden administration started in 2022 in an attempt to hold back China’s ambition'sin AI.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

The rivalry between the U.S. and China has been simmering for years, with Chinese companies like Huawei getting blacklisted because of their work with the People’s Liberation Army. In August 2022, about three months before ChatGPT made AI a household term, Washington expanded its trade bans on Beijing and imposed export controls on Nvidia’s H100 and A100 GPUs. The company responded to this by building a new data center GPU that conformed to U.S. standards specifically for the Chinese market, called the A800, by November of that year. Despite delivering only 70% of the performance of the A100 it was based on, the GPU reportedly still saw great demand from Chinese customers.

However, the A800 only had a relatively short run as the Biden administration once again increased the performance threshold in October 2023, which resulted in the export prohibition of A800 and H800 GPUs to China. This move forced the company to iterate once again, creating new models that it could sell to Chinese companies, like the Nvidia H20. These chips arrived on the market in early 2024, but before the Biden administration ended in January 2025, it proposed even stricter rules called the AI Diffusion Policy. This sorted nations into different tiers based on trust and risk levels — countries in tier 1, which includes the U.S. and its closest allies, have minimal restrictions, while those in tier 3 are effectively barred from receiving advanced AI GPUs containing U.S. technology.

This is problematic for Nvidia, as China is the second-largest computer market in the world t and represented between 20% and 25% of Nvidia's data center sales. The company lobbied the U.S. government to ease AI GPU export restrictions, with Trump reportedly suspending the proposed Nvidia H20 ban after Jensen spent $1 million to have dinner with the president in early April 2025. The White House went ahead anyway and banned the sale of the AI GPU less than a week after that, resulting in a $5.5 billion write-off for the company.

Jensen Huang himself had harsh comments about Washington’s trade ban, saying that “export control was a failure,” and that it had caused the company’s AI GPU market share in China to go from 95% to zero. He even argued that “conceding an entire market the size of China probably does not make a lot of strategic sense, so I think that has already largely backfired.”

But even as Huang was fighting to have the trade ban on the Nvidia H20 chip lifted, he continued praising Trump’s tariff plan, calling it “utterly visionary.” The president eventually reversed the ban three months later, and by December 2025, he had approved Nvidia H200 exports to China, but only if Nvidia pays a 25% fee. The newer Blackwell and Vera Rubin chips remain out of reach for Chinese companies, though — at least on paper.

Allegations that Chinese companies have been breaking Washington’s trade ban and smuggling Nvidia AI GPUs into China have been circulating since June 2023, after Reuters revealed that vendors in Shenzhen could secure A100 chips when asked discreetly. They reportedly bought these chips from the excess stocks sold in the open market or through intermediaries in India, Taiwan, and Singapore. Another story published in January 2024 asserted that the Chinese military and related institutions, state-run data centers, and even universities continue buying banned A100 and H100 chips. Six months after that, accounts of underground networks dedicated to smuggling AI GPUs — even entire servers — through other countries started emerging.

In 2025, an investigative report showed that at least a billion dollars’ worth of Nvidia AI chips were allegedly funneled into China. Some sellers likened the illicit AI GPU trade to a seafood market, with brokers and retailers openly advertising the most advanced Nvidia AI chips online, from RTX 5090 GPUs to complete B200 servers.

Even with all these reports, Huang continued denying that Nvidia’s chips were being smuggled into China. “There’s no evidence of any AI chip diversion,” the then-CEO told reporters at Computex 2025. He also added, “The Grace Blackwell system is nearly two tons, and so you’re not going to be shipping — you’re not going to be putting that in your pocket or your backpack anytime soon. And so, these systems are fairly easy to keep track of... but the important thing is that the countries and the companies that we sell to recognize that diversion is not allowed, and everybody would like to continue to buy Nvidia technology, and so they very well monitor themselves very carefully and they’re quite careful about that.”

In the midst of all these AI chip smuggling rumors, the Bureau of Industry and Security, the agency in charge of enforcing U.S. trade sanctions, was found to be “inadequate” and underfunded, and it has been relying on outdated manual processes to enforce restrictions on Chinese tech companies. Despite that, companies and individuals across the world are being investigated and arrested for bypassing Washington’s export controls.

Singaporean authorities broke up a smuggling ring in early 2025 that smuggled Nvidia GPUs for Chinese AI lab DeepSeek, resulting in a raid of 22 different locations and the arrest of nine people. In October of the same year, a Singapore company called Megaspeed, which was led by Alice Huang, allegedly diverted $2 billion worth of Nvidia chips. Four Americans were then arrested the following month for shipping 400 Nvidia A100s and attempting to send 50 more Nvidia H200 GPUs to China.

An even bigger smuggling scandal unfolded some four months after the arrests, after three Super Micro employees were arrested for smuggling $2.5 billion of Nvidia hardware into China. The suspects included company co-founder Yih-Shyan “Wally” Liaw, although Super Micro itself was not implicated. The Super Micro case spanned the globe, with Taiwanese authorities raiding 12 locations related to the case in May 2026, with another nine sites and six people investigated in June. Jensen Huang urged the company to fix its export control compliance after the arrests and raids, telling the media, “We insist our partners are compliant. We hope that they will enhance and improve their regulatory compliance and prevent that from happening in the future.”

But just five months after he made this statement, one stunning accusation unraveled it all.

On October 29, 2026, The New York Times published a report that Jensen Huang may have been the target of a Chinese spy plot through the executive of a firm who was “close” to him — that executive is Alice Huang. Nvidia denied the accusation. “Megaspeed has been no different than many other regional cloud customers. Jensen’s interactions with Ms. Huang are not unusual or unexpected. Meetings with customers are part of a CEO's job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year,” a company spokesperson told Tom's Hardware. “Our regional cloud customers receive ordinary business information — not sensitive NVIDIA trade secrets — and zero information relevant to national security."

But a little over a week later, U.S. intelligence sources claimed that the former Nvidia chief had an affair with the Megaspeed executive. This is the same Megaspeed that has been accused of smuggling Nvidia chips to the tune of $2 billion. By the evening of Sunday, November 8, Jensen admitted to the affair, although he did not name the third party in his statement.

Many government officials would usually turn a blind eye towards a tech executive’s personal life, but the fact that he is the leader of the U.S.’s premier AI chip maker and that he is also close to the president has caught the attention of authorities. This has led to the U.S. Congress asking him to a closed-door meeting to discuss Nvidia’s “security protocols against foreign adversary espionage” and the FBI investigating his relationship with the alleged Chinese spy.

The admission and allegations led to people digging deeper into Alice Huang. An investigation by The Information revealed that she was connected to a “labyrinth” of companies spanning Singapore, China, and the British Virgin Islands, and that she allegedly helped move around $7.5 billion worth of AI GPU imports. $2 billion was routed from Megaspeed to Speedmatrix, its Malaysia subsidiary, while another $4.6 billion moved directly from the Singaporean company into Shanghai Century Litong, a China-based cloud services company. It has also reportedly bought Nvidia GPUs from other sources, resulting in the estimated total value of its imports.

People close to her also said that she would leverage her relationship with Jensen to customers, often posting pictures with him on her WeChat account, showing potential clients unpublished photos with the Nvidia chief, and even boasting that he would take her to dinner and give her gifts on her birthday. It also seems that Alice Huang was not acting alone. Multiple sources say that Kang Wei, Alice Huang’s husband, was central to the operation to acquire AI GPUs. He even seemingly acknowledged her relationship with Jensen Huang and has jokingly said that she was a personal assistant to the billionaire.

However, it seems that the straw that broke the camel’s back was another allegation that Jensen had an affair with another woman — this time, with Kimberly Powell, the company’s vice president of health care who directly reported to him. Hours after this revelation, the company board announced that Jensen had resigned from all his leadership positions at Nvidia, with employees saying he looked “broken and shattered” as he left the company he spent over three decades building in disgrace. Nvidia is looking for internal and external CEO candidates. Chief financial officer Colette Kress is serving as interim chief executive.

It may be the end of an era, but this does not necessarily spell the end for Jensen Huang. Despite his sudden downfall and quick removal from Nvidia, his status as the king of AI infrastructure remains valuable to the AI industry. Elon Musk even said on X that it “would be an honor” to hire him, and this could ring true for any business that wants to break into the semiconductor space. But does he even want to return?Huang's first public statement after his resignation came on X on Nov. 17, in which the former CEO said he has "outpouring of calls from Nvidia’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO," and that if asked by the company's board, he would be "honored" to take the job."

Over 190,000 shareholders, partners, current and former employees, and fans, including Elon Musk and Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, have signed an online petition to bring him back as the leader of the company. President Donald Trump called for his reinstatement as Nvidia CEO.The board, however, may not see things the same way. Multiple reports suggest that the board isn't considering bringing Huang back, and instead is focusing on a new candidate, the ongoing investigation into Huang, and preparing for national security investigations.

Guide: 42 Switch 1 & 2 Games You Should Check Out In Nintendo's Black Friday eShop Sale (Europe)

📅 Nov 18, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

Every game we scored 9/10 or higher, plus a personal pick

The once one-day event of 'Black Friday' seems to last for almost all of November these days. Anyway, Nintendo has kicked off its digital discounts with an eShop sale in Europe.

The EU Black Friday eShop sale is now live and will be sticking around until 29th November, offering big savings on a bunch of Switch 1 and 2 bangers.

We have assembled the following list to highlight the cream of the crop — who has time to scroll through thousands of games, after all. Below, you'll find every game in Nintendo's Black Friday sale that we awarded a 9/10 or higher. We've also added a personal pick at the end from the games that fall below that threshold, because we just couldn't resist.

As ever, if you're looking to grab some eShop credit before diving in, we've got you covered with the following links from our store.

Please note that some external links on this page are affiliate links, which means if you click them and make a purchase we may receive a small percentage of the sale. Please read our FTC Disclosure for more information.

13 Sentinels: Aegis Rim is a wonderful achievement for dynamic storytelling, as it puts forth a compelling and multifaceted narrative that’ll keep you guessing right up until the very end.

This excellent story, combined with enjoyable combat portions, a striking art style, and some top-notch voice acting make for an experience that you shouldn't miss. It’s the kind of game that’ll have you wishing that you could play it again for the first time, just so all its best elements could be new again.

Ace Combat 7: Skies Unknown is the absolute pinnacle of the series and despite coming to Switch over five years after other platforms, this 'impossible' Switch conversion does very little to degrade the experience. Long-time franchise players and military aviation enthusiasts will be overwhelmed by the fan service at every turn, from craters on the ground to airplanes, liveries, callsigns, and emblems shouting out to previous entries.

We understand the genre is uniquely niche, but if this is your first foray into the franchise, this conversion is a perfect gateway into this rich, revered series. You get tons of content and an epic single-player campaign wrapped up in triple-A presentation that delivers the most comprehensive portable experience ever from Project Aces.

Aegis Defenders is a fantastic game, brilliantly blending the tower defence and platforming genres in a unique way to produce a memorable and enjoyable experience.

Lovable characters, interesting lore, plenty of secrets, engaging gameplay, and gorgeous presentation combine to make this a must-have for your Switch, a real gem on the eShop.

AI: The Somnium Files – nirvanA Initiative is one of the most interesting visual novels we’ve played through in a while. The murder mystery at its heart is brought to life by some great writing and quirky characters alongside the satisfyingly integrated, beautifully balanced Psync puzzle elements.

Even with some minor control issues, there is a lot to love in this game, even if you never picked up the original. Highly recommended if you're even a little bit curious.

Alwa’s Legacy is an excellent example of how to do a proper sequel; it takes everything that Alwa's Awakening did well and builds on it, adds in a few new ideas of its own, and corrects the issues that were previously present.

It may be a little on the short side, but Alwa’s Legacy is the special sort of game that only comes around once in a great while, reminding you of the kind of quality that’s possible when a dedicated crew puts in the time to make a polished and tightly designed final product.

While this turn-based affair might look, move, and feel just like a real board game, Armello is actually a completely original creation — and one that does more than simply doff its cap at the world of tabletop gaming. From the deep tactics of its living board game gameplay to the sheer charm of its worldbuilding and animal character designs, it's a quest filled with back-stabbing, political power plays, and rampaging monsters that’s different each and every time you play. It’s at its absolute best when played in multiplayer, that human factor making for an even more unpredictable battle for the corrupted throne. The Switch version has had its ups and downs since launch, with some updates making things worse, but it's apparently back to being in a playable state on Nintendo's console. As such, you’d be doing yourself a disservice not to add this anthropomorphic tale to your wishlist.

Astral Ascent is a prime example of a game that amounts to more than the sum of its parts. Its strong character design, hi-bit visuals, tight combat, memorable bosses, and broad build variety have all featured in games you’ve probably played before—there’s nothing ‘new’ here.

But to write it off as just 'another one of those' in a crowded genre would be to miss out on one of the most delightful and surprising releases of 2023. Astral Ascent is comfortably one of the best roguelites available on the Switch. Don't miss it.

Catherine: Full Body is a fantastic revamp of a bona fide cult classic. With an excellent new character and several new endings slickly inserted into an already highly entertaining narrative – not to mention a slew of fun new modes – this is the definitive version of an outstanding game.

If you've never played Catherine before, then you're in for an absolute treat, and if you have, we'd say there's enough new content here to make it worth diving in all over again.

An extremely impressive first game from The Wild Gentlemen, Chicken Police - Paint it RED! is one of the best visual novel/adventure games we've played in a long, long time and one hell of an absorbing tale. It looks and runs great on the Switch, with only a couple of really minuscule interface issues which are easily ignored.

At roughly eight or nine hours, the story is surprisingly lengthy, but we were never bored and wanted to investigate every little thing just to wring out more precious droplets of banter and fascination. Chicken Police is a polished, captivating experience and we're very excited for whatever's coming next from this team.

It's difficult to get across exactly why Danganronpa V3: Killing Harmony is so good without spoiling vast swathes of it, so we'll keep it simple. You'll come into the game baffled as to what the writers were thinking with some of these characters, and walk away loving each and every one of them.

There isn't a single moment of slack throughout the whole 40-hour playtime, it has the most extensive post-game of any title in the series, and one of the best endings to any game ever made. Go in blind and we promise you'll be in for the ride of your life.

Even so many years after its 2005 debut, Devil May Cry 3 remains one of the very best action games ever made. It may have aged in places, but that turbo-charged, combo-heavy action feels as fresh today as it did back in the mid-noughties.

The new Freestyle mode – which lets players swap combat styles on the fly at any point during the action – is a genuinely excellent addition to the package, and the ability to play Bloody Palace in local co-op is the cherry on top of a Switch port that should appeal to anyone interested in sampling the devilish delights of this all-time classic.

Dragon Ball FighterZ on the Switch is, simply put, one of the best fighting games we've seen on the system. Arc System Works went the extra mile in capturing the essence of the source material and distilled it into an incredible brawler that has lost nothing in the transition to Nintendo's hybrid console.

The stunning visuals, intense action, and easy-to-master controls make FighterZ a game all fans of the genre should have in their library. If you only play this kind of game casually, it remains a must-own.

Every now and then, a game comes along that captures our hearts and reminds us why we love the medium in the first place. Forager features wonderfully designed crafting mechanics, addictive progression systems and more charm than you can possibly handle. Although it has very minor drawbacks, there's enough good stuff present here for us to confidently recommend adding Forager to your collection.

Heretic + Hexen is yet another slam dunk for Nightdive Studios. This new release revamps both titles with modern controls, bonus content, and thoughtful changes to the core design that make each game a delight to play.

Granted, these are still FPS titles from the mid-'90s, so your mileage will definitely vary, but for returning fans and those with a particular fondness for old-school 'boomer shooters', you really can't go wrong. Now let's get a native Switch 2 port with 120fps please, Nightdive.

An absolute pleasure from start to finish, what Kaze and the Wild Masks lacks in originality it makes up for in the strength of its level design, responsive controls, kinetic move set and attractive visuals. Excellent, action-packed platforming through and through, with great gameplay variety and gimmicks that don’t compromise on what the game is best at — challenging, fast-paced obstacle courses and deviously hidden secret areas.

Easiest sell? Kaze and the Wild Masks is to Donkey Kong Country what Freedom Planet was to Sonic the Hedgehog. Don’t miss this one.

It may be over in the blink of an eye, but Kraino Origins proves itself to be a well-crafted and deeply enjoyable old-school action platformer while it lasts. There’s a little bit of Mega Man in here, a little more Castlevania, some Super Mario Bros. 3, but Kraino doesn’t feel overly derivative of such titles, largely because of its excellent level design. With some excellent 8-bit pixel art, this is an affordable and brief entry in the neo-retro genre, and one that we would definitely recommend.

The original La-Mulana was a masterpiece in its own right, but we’d contend that it’s been edged out by the sequel. What we have here is an expertly-paced, crushingly difficult, and utterly mystifying adventure that constantly beckons you to explore deeper and acquaint yourself with its unique charms. La-Mulana 2 definitely isn’t for everybody – if you consider yourself an impatient or clumsy player, steer clear – but those who put in the time and effort to crack this nut will be deeply satisfied that they did so. We’d give La-Mulana 2 a high recommendation for anybody looking for a deep and challenging new Metroidvania for their Switch; it’s an acquired taste, but one you will come to savour.

Mega Man X Legacy Collection is a fantastic re-release of several must-play gaming classics, presenting them as authentically as possible while still including a few modern features on top that help to improve the overall experience and keep it from feeling antiquated.

Throw in the new X Challenge mode and an enormous archive of museum content and this stands as the definitive way to play the Mega Man X games in the modern era. Four fantastic games, a bevvy of extra content, and the ability to play at home or on the go — nothing not to like here.

Mega Man Zero/ZX Legacy Collection is everything that you could’ve hoped it to be. This is ultimately six great Mega Man games presented to you with a slew of customisable features, extra content, and quality-of-life updates.

If you’re a fan of either Mega Man or side-scrolling action games in general, you owe it to yourself to give this release a go and see what all the fuss is about. These are hard and occasionally frustrating games, but they offer up some rewarding, action-heavy gameplay that even today stands among the best of its class. Don’t pass this collection up.

Monster Hunter Generations Ultimate may lack the accessibility that made Monster Hunter: World such a smash hit, but it more than makes up for it by being a sort of ‘greatest hits’ collection of the high points of the series, giving you hundreds of hours of content to play through. Couple this with the HD visuals, easy-to-use multiplayer, and the ability to play the full experience on the go, and you’ve got a game that will appeal to both veterans and newcomers alike.

It may not necessarily represent the future of the series, but this is a fantastic experience in its own right and a worthy follow-up to the 3DS original, and one that no Switch owner will want to be without, even if series newcomers might want to start with Rise first.

Okami HD is an utterly fantastic piece of software, and we feel you’d be doing yourself a disservice to pass on it. It's a 40-hour adventure that emulates Zelda wonderfully, adds in plenty of memorable mechanics, features one of the most beautiful art styles in gaming, and is completely playable on the go, to boot.

It may be showing its age a bit visually and its combat is sometimes a little on the easy side, but Okami is an important, fun, and notable landmark in gaming history — and one of the easiest recommendations we can make for your Switch library.

Orbitals set out to do something very specific: deliver an action-packed co-operative game while building a new world inspired by anime classics. On those two notes, it smashes it out of the park. The puzzles not only last just the right amount of time, but we were consistently delighted by the clever ways the strict set of tools were utilised, and the many fun ways you interact with this fantastically realised anime world.

Our main complaint is that we wanted much more of it, and while the gameplay itself feels perfectly paced, the somewhat abrupt ending left us wishing more time was spent establishing the stakes and motivations of the story.

Ultimately, Orbitals is a truly phenomenal co-operative title and one of the best ways to spend an evening with a friend this year. With phenomenal visuals, thrilling mechanics, and the brilliant characters and story, this is the new high bar for co-op games.

AI Made Writing Code Cheap. Getting It Reviewed Now Takes 5x Longer, Says LinearB’s CEO

📅 Nov 18, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

AI, Web3, Cybersecurity, Startup Funding & Enterprise SaaS. Top Journalist, Analyst & Thought Leadership Media Leader.

AI, Web3, Cybersecurity, Startup Funding & Enterprise SaaS. Top Journalist, Analyst & Thought Leadership Media Leader.

AI, Web3, Cybersecurity, Startup Funding & Enterprise SaaS. Top Journalist, Analyst & Thought Leadership Media Leader.

A developer using an AI assistant can open a pull request in minutes, yet the change still sits in a queue until a human reviewer picks it up. That is why agent-written pull requests wait 17.6 hours for a first review against 3.4 hours for human ones, even as enterprises spent $4.0 billion on AI coding tools in 2025, seven times the year before.

Today we sit down with Ori Keren, co-founder and CEO of LinearB, to discuss how the company grew from engineering dashboards into a context layer for agents, how it sells to boards that want proof of AI's return and where developer productivity goes once agents write much of the code.

Ishan Pandey: Welcome to Behind the Startup, Ori. Tell us about your journey and what made you build LinearB in the first place?

Ori Keren: Thanks for having me, Ishan. I started writing code as a kid, programming in BASIC on a Sinclair Spectrum in 1987, and I got my first developer job in 2000. From there I moved into management. I ran an engineering group at Interwise, which AT&T acquired, and then I was VP of R&D at CloudLock, which Cisco acquired in 2016. That's where I met Dan Lines, my co-founder.

What stayed with me from those years is how blind software development is. You run a team of a hundred engineers, and every week the business asks when something will ship or why it's late. You answer from gut feel and status meetings. Meanwhile, every answer is sitting in Git, in Jira and in your CI system, just never connected.

So in 2019, Dan and I started LinearB to connect it. We wanted to give engineering leaders real data on how their teams deliver, instead of gut feel, and then help them act on it. Helping teams act on the data is still what drives everything we build, and today those teams include agents.

Ishan Pandey: LinearB started in 2019 by giving engineering leaders delivery metrics, yet you have now rebuilt the platform around a knowledge graph of the whole software delivery lifecycle. What did you see in customer data over the past year that told you this called for a rebuild of the company's core?

Ori Keren: Two things, and they showed up in the data at the same time.

The first was that AI made writing code cheap but didn't make delivery faster. Our benchmarks cover 8.1 million pull requests from 4,800 teams. AI-assisted pull requests are about 2.6 times larger than unassisted ones. Pull requests opened by agents wait 17.6 hours for a first review, against 3.4 hours for human ones. The bottleneck simply moved downstream, into review, merge and ownership.

The second was why agents struggle. An agent starts every task cold. It has a good idea of the code, but it doesn't have the business context. It doesn't know that this service had two incidents last month, that this file has been rewritten five times this quarter, or who owns it. We had all of that, linked from ticket to release, for every customer.

That's when it clicked. Everyone else is focused on writing code. We hold a knowledge graph of everything happening across delivery, and that's exactly what agents and teams need. A dashboard can't hand that context to an agent, so we rebuilt LinearB around the graph itself. Context is the new king.

Ishan Pandey: When you raised your Series B in 2022, LinearB served more than 5,000 development teams. How has the customer base grown since then and which kind of company is now expanding fastest on the platform?

Ori Keren: We've moved up market. In 2022, a lot of our growth came bottom up, from engineering managers at fast-moving tech companies. Today our core is the enterprise, meaning organizations with hundreds or thousands of engineers, several AI coding tools running at once, and a board asking what it's getting for the spend. We're also seeing strong growth among healthcare organizations.

The pattern is consistent. A company adopts Copilot here, Cursor there and Claude Code somewhere else. Within a quarter or two, leadership realizes it can't answer basic questions, like whether the code holds up, where it's working and what it's costing. That's when they come to us, and that's when they expand.

Kraken is a good example of what that looks like. They used our MCP with an AI assistant to find out what was slowing their code reviews. It turned out to be time zones and reviewer availability, not change size. Within four months, they cut review time at the 90th percentile by more than half.

Ishan Pandey: Boards and CFOs now ask directly whether AI coding spend is paying off. How has that changed who signs a LinearB contract, from the VP of engineering to the CFO or CIO, along with how a deal is won?

Ori Keren: The SVP of engineering or CTO is still our executive buyer.

Who they answer to. Ken Ringdahl, the CTO at Emburse, puts our charts straight into his board decks because his board asks specifically about AI use and ROI. That's now normal.

There are a lot of company-wide AI initiatives now, driven by the CFO or CEO, and in the companies we work with, engineering is usually where AI spend is highest.

So finance is in the room far more often. Engineering leaders bring us in because they need numbers that hold up in front of a CFO, not a vanity metric from a vendor's own dashboard.

That changes how a deal is won. Five years ago, we won by showing a better cycle-time chart. Today we win by answering the finance question in the evaluation itself. We connect the data, and within days we show which teams are getting value from AI, which aren't, and what each delivered change costs. Token spend makes this sharper. In our 2026 AI benchmarks, which cover 253 engineering organizations, developers at the 90th percentile now spend $35.20 per coding day on tokens, up nearly 75% in three months. When a CFO sees that line, the conversation moves fast.

Ishan Pandey: LinearB built an audience through the Dev Interrupted podcast and free developer tools long before Gartner gave the category a Magic Quadrant. How does that community-led motion now work alongside enterprise sales and which channel brings in your largest customers today?

Ori Keren: Dev Interrupted was never meant as a lead generator. We started it because engineering leaders had nowhere to talk about the craft of running engineering. That trust turned out to be our moat. When a category gets a Magic Quadrant, every buyer suddenly has a shortlist. Our edge is that many of the people on the buying side have listened to the show for years, used our free tools, or borrowed our benchmarks for their own planning.

Today the two motions feed each other. Community and free tools create familiarity, often with a director or a staff engineer. Benchmarks and research give the champion something credible to take upstairs. Enterprise sales then turns that into an organization-wide rollout with security review, procurement and an ROI case.

Our largest deals close through our enterprise sales team, and when we trace them back, someone inside almost always knew LinearB before the first sales call. That's the compounding effect we're after.

Ishan Pandey: Your effort skill sends simple changes through cheaper agent runs while giving risky changes more care and more tokens. How do you price a product whose value is partly measured in tokens saved and what will the next skills for review and merge add for customers?

Ori Keren: First, a clarification. The effort skill isn't a cost-cutting tool that happens to touch quality. It's a judgment tool. It looks at a change's complexity and risk, using the full knowledge graph, and decides how hard the agent should work. Sometimes that means fewer tokens. On a fragile payments service, it means more, with careful, tested edits. The goal is the right effort on each change.

That's why we don't price on tokens saved. If we took a cut of savings, we'd be rewarded for making agents cheap rather than for making delivery better. Customers judge us on the cost of each delivered change, not the raw token bill.

The next skills go where the bottleneck now sits, in review and merge. They'll use the same context to help teams decide where human attention is needed and what can move faster. After that comes governance of AI-written code and spend optimization.

Ishan Pandey: Gartner sizes the developer productivity insight market at about $400 million while enterprises already spend billions on AI coding tools. How large can this category become once it measures and guides agents as well as people over the next three years?

Ori Keren: The $400 million figure describes the developer productivity insight category, platforms that give engineering leaders visibility into how their teams deliver software. We've always operated in that category, and we've also always gone beyond it. Our philosophy has been to explore, measure, act, and the act part now shows up in our agent skills.

Once a company spends that much on agents, a layer that decides how those agents should work, where they should spend effort and whether their output is safe to ship isn't a reporting tool anymore. It's part of the delivery system, like CI/CD or observability. So the right comparison isn't to other dashboards. It's a share of total spend on software delivery, human and agent combined.

What I'm confident about is the direction. We think it's time for the category to stop being something leaders look at once a month and become something agents consult on every change.

Ishan Pandey: For CTOs and VPs of engineering whose boards will ask them this year to prove AI's return, what is the first thing you would tell them to measure and which older metric should they stop reporting?

Ori Keren: Measure the cost per effective delivered change, not code generated, pull requests opened or lines accepted from an assistant. An effective change is one that merged, shipped and didn't come back as rework. Take what you spend on people and tokens, and divide it by those changes. You want effective changes trending up and the cost of each one trending down. That's the number that tells a board whether AI is paying off, and it holds up when finance pushes on it.

Emburse tracks exactly this. Over seven months, most of its code moved to AI, and its cost per effective pull request fell about 35%.

Right next to it, track what each model costs against the quality of the code it produces. The differences are bigger than most teams expect. Kraken found that two engineers can ship the same work while one burns thousands of dollars in tokens and the other spends hundreds, depending on which models they use and how.

Then stop reporting raw throughput, like pull requests or commits per developer, and above all, stop reporting AI adoption rates. Telling a board that 90% of your engineers use AI says nothing about return.

Inside engineering, though, keep measuring how work flows through your software factory. The bottlenecks haven't gone away. They've moved to review and release.

For CTOs and VPs of engineering heading into a board meeting, the practical takeaway is his metric. Cost per effective delivered change puts people and token spend over work that merged, shipped and stayed fixed, which gives a CFO a number to test. With AI coding spend compounding and the measurement category growing more than 40% a year, I expect the teams that adopt this kind of accounting early to have the easiest budget conversations of 2027. Leaders who want to compare their own teams can start with LinearB's free benchmarks report or the LinearB platform.

AI agents without engineers: why the next era of AI belongs to non-technical teams

📅 Nov 18, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

Over the past three years, enterprise software followed a predictable playbook: embed a generative chat widget into every existing SaaS interface and call it an AI strategy.

The resulting reality inside most organizations, however, has been underwhelming. While individual employees occasionally consult personal copilots to draft an email or summarize a document, these interactions remain strictly “single-player.” The context generated during those sessions sits locked inside private browser tabs, disconnected from the rest of the organization. When another team member needs the same output, the loop resets. More critically, when complex initiatives require cross-functional context, asynchronous coordination, and direct tool execution, isolated bots inevitably stall.

Bridging the gap between personal productivity assistants and true organizational leverage requires a fundamental architectural rethink: moving away from isolated copilots and toward shared, multi-player AI agents for business that operate directly alongside human teams.

Among the platforms pioneering this paradigm shift, Zenzap has emerged as a distinct model, approaching autonomous agency not as an engineering project or an isolated backend script, but as a native, shared team member embedded directly within everyday communication channels.

Most corporate implementations of AI fail to generate durable compound value because of three structural flaws:

Resolving these tensions requires an environment where an AI agent for business is neither a complex developer-only tool nor an opaque personal secret, but a visible, accountable participant in collaborative work.

For autonomous agents to scale across an enterprise, domain experts must be able to deploy them without submitting an IT ticket.

Zenzap addresses this bottleneck by stripping away the developer requirement entirely. Rather than demanding bespoke code or complex orchestration frameworks, the platform enables business operators to build your own AI agents without code in a single step.

This shifts agent development from centralized engineering teams to frontline managers. A marketing director can instantiate an agent dedicated solely to competitive ad tracking, while an operations lead can stand up a fulfillment triage agent, each tailored with specific responsibilities, operational parameters, and resource access without writing a line of code.

Where most automation platforms rely on rigid dashboards or complex node graphs, Zenzap situates agency within a native conversational workspace.

Instead of isolating agents on standalone dashboards, Zenzap integrates them into multi-user chat environments. Multiple team members can enter a shared channel with an agent, issue instructions in natural language or via voice notes, and observe the agent’s execution steps in real time.

Because the agent operates within the team stream, context is cumulative. When an agent is corrected or given updated guidance, it retains that operational memory across subsequent team exchanges and connected systems. If an account manager refines an onboarding workflow once, the entire team benefits from that institutional retention without repeating the instruction.

Chat-based AI is only as useful as its ability to act. An agent that merely suggests copy without updating the underlying records quickly becomes digital clutter.

Zenzap connects conversational direction to downstream operational execution through integrations with over 2,000 workplace applications. When a team discusses client updates, resource reallocations, or scheduling conflicts, the agent can translate conversational decisions into real-world database updates, notifications, and workflow actions across the company’s software stack.

However, granting software autonomous execution rights inside enterprise systems requires strict boundaries. Zenzap enforces a three-tier permission model across every integrated tool:

To meet corporate compliance requirements, Zenzap aligns with SOC 2, HIPAA, GDPR, and ISO 27001 standards, alongside a structural data policy ensuring customer and organizational inputs are never ingested to train public foundation models.

The enterprise software landscape does not need another isolated chat window or another brittle automation dashboard that requires a team of software engineers to maintain.

The future of productivity lies in collaborative agentic infrastructure, systems where non-technical operators can spin up dedicated digital coworkers, invite their teams into the room, and direct complex execution across thousands of tools under rigorous governance. By grounding agency in shared human conversation, Zenzap provides a blueprint for how organizations can finally move past the experimental pilot stage and put autonomous AI to work where business actually happens.

Circle Internet Group vs. Strategy: Crypto's Brutal Sell-Off Is Exposing a Critical Difference Between These 2 Stocks

📅 Nov 18, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

The cryptocurrency downturn is putting two fundamentally different business models to the test, raising questions about which offers investors a more sustainable path to long-term returns.

The ongoing cryptocurrency bear market is exposing fundamental differences between businesses operating in the digital asset economy. Circle Internet Group (CRCL -5.24%) and Strategy (MSTR -6.34%) offer investors two distinct ways to gain exposure to the industry, but their financial performance depends on very different factors.

Circle is building the financial infrastructure behind digital payments through its USDC (USDC -0.01%) stablecoin, generating revenue primarily from interest earned on its reserves. Strategy, meanwhile, has transformed itself from an enterprise software company into a Bitcoin (BTC +0.06%) treasury business, leveraging capital markets to accumulate increasingly large holdings of the cryptocurrency.

While both companies stand to benefit from the long-term adoption of digital assets, their contrasting business models, capital structures, and exposure to cryptocurrency volatility could have significant implications for shareholder returns heading into 2027.

With services spanning 185 countries, Circle is positioned to benefit from the growing integration of blockchain technology into traditional finance. Unlike many cryptocurrency businesses, Circle does not depend directly on rising digital asset prices to drive revenue. Instead, it earns the majority of its revenue from interest generated on USDC reserves.

In the 12 months ended Sept. 30, 2026, revenue reached nearly $3 billion, representing year-over-year growth of approximately 25.7%. Net income totaled $462.9 million, translating to a profit margin of roughly 15.4%. The expanding use of stablecoins for payments and financial settlement provides Circle with a structural growth opportunity that extends beyond speculative cryptocurrency trading.

As of December 2025, Circle maintained a debt-to-equity ratio of 0.0 and a current ratio of 1.0. The company generated approximately $529.7 million in free cash flow during fiscal 2025. However, stock-based compensation represented 104.4% of operating cash flow, warranting closer scrutiny of the quality of its cash generation.

Although Strategy continues to operate its enterprise analytics software business, its investment thesis increasingly centers on accumulating Bitcoin. The company utilizes a combination of common stock, preferred securities, and debt financing to expand its Bitcoin holdings, providing shareholders with exposure to the cryptocurrency through a traditional equity structure.

Over the latest 12-month reporting period, revenue reached approximately $495.1 million, representing year-over-year growth of 4.2%. However, Strategy reported a net loss of approximately $13.7 billion, primarily reflecting declines in the fair value of its Bitcoin holdings. The disparity between revenue and net income illustrates how much Bitcoin's price movements now overshadow the financial performance of its software business.

As of December 2025, Strategy maintained a debt-to-equity ratio of 0.2 and a current ratio of 5.6. Despite these seemingly favorable balance sheet metrics, the company recorded negative free cash flow of $112.5 million in fiscal 2025. With limited internal cash generation, Strategy remains heavily dependent on external financing to support its Bitcoin accumulation strategy.

One of Circle's primary risks is intensifying competition. Efforts to formalize stablecoin regulation, most notably through the GENIUS Act, lend legitimacy to the industry but also open the door for banks, payment processors, and fintech companies to issue competing stablecoins, potentially eroding Circle's market share and profitability. Circle is also sensitive to interest rates, as falling short-term Treasury yields could reduce reserve income unless offset by growth in USDC circulation.

Strategy faces a different set of risks. The company frequently issues new shares to fund Bitcoin purchases, which can dilute the ownership of existing shareholders. While selling new shares has historically worked in Strategy's favor during bull markets, a prolonged bear market makes this approach less effective. As Bitcoin's price declines, Strategy risks having to issue additional shares to fund further purchases, potentially diluting existing shareholders without delivering a corresponding increase in per-share value.

While Circle appears more reasonably valued based on its P/S ratio, Strategy currently offers a lower multiple relative to its future earnings estimates.

Valuation metrics include sourcing from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from other data providers.

Investors should note that the Forward P/E compares the current stock price to future earnings estimates. The P/S ratio measures the company market cap against sales over the past twelve months.

Despite Circle's relatively expensive forward price-to-earnings ratio of 53.2 compared to Strategy's 6.5, I believe Circle offers the more compelling investment opportunity heading into 2027. Strategy's seemingly attractive earnings multiple warrants caution, as its profitability is heavily influenced by fluctuations in Bitcoin's price rather than the underlying performance of its software business. Circle also trades at just 5.4 times sales, compared to Strategy's 93.1, although traditional valuation metrics are less useful when evaluating a Bitcoin treasury company.

Ultimately, the deciding factor for me is the sustainability of each company's business model. Stablecoins represent one of the most practical applications of blockchain technology, with opportunities extending across cross-border payments, commercial transactions, and institutional financial settlement. Circle can capitalize on this growing adoption regardless of whether Bitcoin enters another bull market.

Strategy could deliver substantial returns if Bitcoin rebounds in 2027. However, its dependence on capital markets and potential shareholder dilution introduce additional risks that investors would not encounter by simply owning Bitcoin. While Circle faces competitive pressures and a demanding earnings valuation of its own, I prefer its ability to generate revenue from the broader adoption of digital assets rather than relying on their price appreciation.

Rahm Emanuel and Chris Christie agree on one thing: character will decide 2028

📅 Nov 18, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

Good morning. Moments before I interviewed Bristol Myers Squibb CEO Chris Boerner on stage at the Fortune 500 Innovation Forum yesterday, a news alert flashed across my phone: The United States had officially lost its measles elimination status, a distinction it had held for more than 25 years. More than 5,400 cases have been reported this year alone under an administration that has fired scientists, disregarded public health protocols, and undermined faith in vaccines.

I asked Boerner, whose drug company does not make the vaccine, what he made of the news. “Very troubling,” he said, noting that America’s enviable ecosystem in biotechnology and pharmaceuticals is a benefit, not a birthright. “It rests on respect for science.”

That fireside chat took place around the same time that Jensen Huang said he’d be “honored” to return as CEO of Nvidia, as if multiple affairs and potential security violations paled next to the “outpouring of calls” for him to return. The board declined. Good call.

My conversations over the past two days reinforced that character matters, in leadership and in life. Rocket Companies founder and chairman Dan Gilbert talked about his extensive investments in transforming downtown Detroit—including The Department at Hudson’s Detroit, where the event was held. He made a compelling case for “more-than-profit” businesses that deliver financially while contributing to the communities in which they operate. He also talked about how his stroke shifted his priorities as a leader and what it will take to realize his dream of making Detroit—and Cleveland—two of the world’s top cities. As for the midterms, Gilbert said, “I hope these guys can shake hands and figure out how to get things done.”

That sentiment was echoed by former Chicago Mayor Rahm Emanuel, a Democrat, and former New Jersey Governor Chris Christie, a Republican. Here is a link to our conversation. Both politicians suggested creating ethics laws that would require politicians to put their assets in a blind trust and ban stock trading and investments in prediction markets.

Christie declared that “the Trump era is over.” He cited opportunities for bipartisan things to get done. They both predicted that character will be the deciding issue in 2028, or as Christie said, “a president who stands for much more than GDP.”

“America needs to close this chapter of pitting one American against the other,” Emanuel said.

Government matters, but tackling tough problems is what leaders do. Optum CEO Patrick Conway knows that he’s in a health services industry that’s not loved, where customers struggle to pay. Having held senior roles at a health insurer, a hospital system, and in government, he knows that “the system doesn’t work today,” but he’s optimistic that digitization and simplification could transform the patient experience. One reason he continues to work weekends as a practicing physician is that he wants to understand how issues like affordability are affecting patients and “prevent those stories from occurring in the future.”Contact CEO Daily via Diane Brady at diane.brady@fortune.com

Nvidia chair says board does not plan to bring back Jensen Huang as CEO

On Nvidia’s first earnings call since Huang resigned, Chair Harvey Jones said the board does not intend to reinstate him and would not take questions about his departure or the ongoing investigation into his conduct. Nvidia reported $115.8 billion in quarterly revenue, above Wall Street estimates, but analysts did not ask about its sales through Singapore or a reported SEC investigation into possibly misguiding investors.

DoorDash’s bid for Instacart puts board ties in focus

DoorDash has agreed to buy grocery-delivery rival Instacart for $17 billion, and partners at one investment firm, Sequoia Capital, sit on both companies’ boards. Fortune found similar ties at other investment firms, and legal experts say these arrangements can make rivals less willing to compete and more likely to merge.

Fund managers make their biggest cut to tech investments since 2006

Fund managers reduced their exposure to tech stocks by the most since June 2006, according to Bank of America’s latest survey. Some 52% expect at least one major cloud company to cut capital spending within six months, despite Wall Street forecasts that spending will rise sharply next year.

Bitcoin's post-Nvidia earnings rally faded within 35 minutes as ETF outflows and weak demand threaten a sustained recovery.

In its first earnings report since Jensen Huang’s departure, Nvidia reported $115.8 billion in fiscal third-quarter revenue, up 103% from a year earlier, and topping the $109.1 billion Bloomberg analyst consensus.

Nvidia projected $130 billion in fourth-quarter revenue, plus or minus 3%, above the $125.2 billion analyst estimate Yahoo Finance reported. The forecast covers a quarter with an extra week and assumes zero data center compute revenue from China.

Nvidia’s board accepted Huang’s resignation effective Nov. 11 and disclosed it Nov. 12, according to the company’s SEC filing. Colette Kress took over as interim CEO while retaining her job as chief financial officer.

Nvidia released the figures at 4:20 p.m. ET, and Bitcoin traded close to $64,000 at the end of the one-minute interval before the report. It touched $64,602.98 during the 4:33 p.m. minute and was back to $64,246.47 by 4:55 p.m., still about $244 above its pre-release level.

Separately, Nvidia traded at $157.83 at 4:56:47 p.m. ET, up 1.52% from its $155.46 regular-session close.

Traders can withdraw those orders, so order book size only indicates how much buying might materialize. If the lower edge of the range gives way, Glassnode pointed to the June low near $58,500 and the aggregate realized price near $53,700, based on the prices at which coins last moved.

This smell startup says its AI nose is as good as a human’s

📅 Nov 18, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

Osmo’s smell model is already being used in the fragrance industry. But are medical diagnostics and threat detection a sniff too far?

In a lab near Newark Airport in New Jersey, a team of around 30 experienced human sniffers are slowly working their way through every odor on Earth. Their careful notes—“nutty,” “peachy,” “marine”—are cross-referenced with a chemical analysis to create a rich set of training data for what AI startup Osmo calls the world’s first foundation model for smell. The company’s goal, says founder Alex Wiltschko, is “to give computers a sense of smell.”

“Scent molecules are really the only language most species on this planet can speak,” he says. “Most species can’t communicate with sound or visually, so it truly is Earth’s original language. And it’s incredibly powerful for us, from a memory and an emotional standpoint. You can smell something once and remember it for the rest of your life. You can smell something on the street and be pulled back to high school.”

In the last few months, Wiltschko claims, Osmo’s model has achieved “human-level olfactory intelligence.” The company’s definition of this is that the model is about as good as the average person at detecting and discriminating between smells, and about as good as a junior perfume designer at creating them. It says its technology is already being used in the fragrance industry to help brands design and manufacture new scents. Last month, the company says, Osmo’s AI model outperformed in-house perfumers at one of the world’s largest consumer goods companies. Wiltschko believes it could be deployed eventually for threat detection at airports, for example, or diagnosing diseases.

Wiltschko spun the startup out of his work at Google Brain, the search giant’s former AI research lab, in 2023, and he is running the same playbook as AI startups in other domains: Throw a lot of data at difficult problems, and see what happens. The challenge with scent, Wiltschko says, is that there was a dearth of good data. Before Osmo, there were fewer than 200,000 human descriptions of smells in existing databases, by his count. Plus, the chemical sensor devices needed to collect data are expensive, and the fragrance industry is secretive about its work on olfactory science.

A lot of the company’s work has been in creating its own dataset of more than 10 million human labels and 800 million “scent tokens,” which describe the exact molecules and concentrations that go into creating specific odors. Osmo uses spectrometers and other chemical sensors, running around the clock, to break down the molecular makeup of everything from fruit and flowers to pantry  staples and organs. A team of around 70 trained data labelers in the US and overseas spend their days sniffing things and writing down what they smell like, using a standardized fragrance vocabulary.

Mapping out scents in this way is throwing out some unlikely parallels. In the same way that changing the order of words can drastically influence the meaning of a sentence, rearranging scent molecules in different proportions can drastically alter the smells humans perceive. “The scent tokens that define the smell of a newborn baby have massive overlap with the scent tokens in a fresh plate of cooked spaghetti,” Wiltschko says. (Specifically Barilla brand spaghetti, he says, which perhaps raises some questions for the people at the pasta factory.)

The company also creates its own scents, using a smell-printing robot the size of a school bus that mixes ingredients according to precise formulas to make samples for Osmo’s own research and fragrances for paying customers. It can design and print scents to order based on a ChatGPT-style prompt. Wiltschko flipped open his laptop to show me how the AI model worked. He opened a text box on screen, and I asked him to generate a fragrance that smelled like a Portuguese custard tart (we were in Lisbon for Web Summit), aimed at 18- to 23-year-old men. The system spent a few minutes cogitating, then generated three options for potential scent profiles that matched the brief (creamy, coconutty, fruity) and the molecules needed to create them. If I’d continued with the ordering process, my signature L’Eau de Custard would have been ready about a week later.

Osmo’s technology has already been used to create retail fragrances, including for giants like Procter & Gamble. The Gates Foundation, which invested $5 million when Osmo launched, later gave the company a $3.5 million grant to assess molecules that repel disease-carrying insects, and Osmo identified eight substances that were more repellent than DEET. Osmo has also worked with StockX, the online clothing marketplace, on using smell to spot counterfeit sneakers by detecting differences in the chemical composition of the materials used in the shoes.

But not everyone is convinced by the technology or the company’s big claims. Avery Gilbert, a smell scientist and author of What the Nose Knows, has been sharply critical of Osmo on his Substack, arguing that some of its marketing claims are undocumented, and that its patent filings still rely on human sensory panels and perfumers, rather than AI. “This heavy reliance on human sensory judgments seems odd for a company premised on super-cool AI,” he wrote in March. A representative for Osmo did not respond in time for publication.

Michael Schmuker, a former professor of neural computation at the University of Hertfordshire who has previously consulted for Osmo, says the company’s technology is an achievement. With colleagues, he created an open-source, reverse-engineered version of Osmo’s 2023 model, but it lacks the reams of data the company has collected since.

But even with all this smell data, Osmo may be missing some of the factors that make human olfaction unique, Schmuker says. “Smell is super complex. Context is very important for smell. The same molecule may evoke a different association depending on context,” he says. “[The smell of] a French cheese like Camembert is partly the same molecule as in used nappies. You don’t confuse the two because of the context.”

In a controlled setting like a fragrance lab, this lack of context may not matter so much. But it could have an impact if Osmo’s technology becomes, as Wiltschko suggests, the “olfactive channel” for AI world models. Imagine a machine that could sniff out spoilage in food on a production line, or detect tumors through smell the way dogs have been trained to do in pilot studies.

For that to happen, sensor technology will need to get a lot better, Schmuker says. The models will need to keep improving. Medical diagnostics is the biggest prize.

“There’s a lot of history of companies that have gone directly at that mountain peak and, unfortunately, not been successful, because it is very expensive and it is very difficult,” Wiltschko says. "So what we’re doing is building this foundation at the foothills of all these mountains. We’re sending expeditions up to the mountains, doing explorations, and basically smelling the whole world.”

Ten years after AlphaGo’s match against Go champion Lee Sedol, today’s AI still isn’t tapping into the machinery that made that win possible.

Tallinn TV Beats Prizes: ‘Intimacy on Prescription,’ About Sex Therapy, Bags Top Award: ‘Good TV Is Very Connected to Good Sex’

📅 Nov 18, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

“Good TV is very connected to good sex; it shows that you are free, and this freedom is very important to us,” said Czech producer Karolina Zalabakova at Tuesday night’s TV Beats Awards ceremony in Tallinn, Estonia, where her project “Intimacy on Prescription” scooped the Council of Europe’s coveted €50,000 ($56,000) Series Co-Production Development Award.

In her acceptance speech last night, the emotional Zalabakova hinted both at the topic of her show – sex therapy in 1970s Czechoslovakia – and at her government’s current attempt to crush media freedom through an unpopular reform of its public service media. Related Stories MS NOW Has 2026 Midterm Elections Coverage: Here's How to Watch Election Night Results Live Online Free UFC 334 Livestream: How to Watch Gane vs. Hokit Online

“Today, Nov. 17, marks the [37th] anniversary of the Velvet Revolution so it has an even stronger meaning. We needed to have a good excuse not to be demonstrating in Prague and this [award] proves us right,” said Zalabakova who was on hand in the Estonian capital with her production partner Lukaš Garkulák.

Inspired by the real life story of Stanislav Kratochvíl, a pioneer of couples’ sex therapy, the dramedy, written by Kristina Májová, is set in a psychiatric clinic, where couples are invited to say out loud what society, marriage and shame have taught them to hide.Speaking at the awards ceremony on behalf of his co-jurors Alessia Sonaglioni of the Council of Europe Eurimages and Gudny Hummelvoll of Norway’s Hummelfilm, Graham Begg of the UK’s Rainmaker Content said “the award goes to a project selected for reasons including but not limited to its originality, universal theme, depiction of 1970’s Eastern European society from a different perspective and self-evident level of research undertaken by the producers as part of their development of the series to date.”

In a totally different genre, the Irish-Canadian spy thriller “Tanner” created by Keith Hodder, brought home both the Göteborg Film Festival’’s TV Drama Vision Select Award and the Conecta 2027 Award.

Produced by Bernie Hoban and Darach Ó Tuairisg of Fíbín Films (“Boglands”) in co-production with Canadian powerhouse Rhombus Media (“The Sympathizer”), the show turns on a former Irish intelligence officer who returns home to investigate a missing teenager and uncovers a tech-powered conspiracy.

A fourth industry award – the Midpoint Talent Award – was handed out to “The Inheritance”, produced by Belgium’s Panenka (“This is Not a Murder Mystery”). The psychological thriller, set against the world of animal welfare and hunting, is penned by Alexandra Jans and Jan Van Dyck.

At the closing ceremony of the 6th TV Beats series market, part of the Industry @ Tallinn & Baltic Event, co-heads Petri Kemppinen and Roosa Toivonen also handed out to ‘the ‘Queen of Nordic drama’ Piv Bernth (“The Killing,” “Blackwater”), the TV Beats Honorary Award, which she shared with the creative trio of the German hit “Babylon Berlin”: Tom Tykwer, Achim von Borries and Henk Handloegten.

Receiving the recognition from the hands of Koivonen, the pioneer of the Nordic Noir and former head of drama at DR, said: “When I arrived at DR Drama [in the mid-1980s], the TV station was very old fashioned and really boring! It changed over the years, and I was so lucky as a producer to be at the right place at the right time.”

Thanking DR “for teaching me everything I know,” “The Killing” creator Søren Sveistrup and actress Sofie Gråbøl among others, she confirmed that she will be closing her current outfit- – ITV Studios’-backed Apple Tree Production – in the New Year and deliver to the Danish pubcaster a last show [“The Best of Families”]. “That closes a cycle and it’s a really good point to start [a new one],” she said.

Commenting on this year’s slate of 10 TV projects selected from 50 submissions across Europe, Begg said “the quality of the pitches was the testament of the quality of the event attended by a mix of top tier, emerging and seasoned producers.”“I’ve been at TV Beats since its inception, and this edition was by far the strongest,” said Cia Edström of the Göteborg Film festival’s TV Drama Vision.

Nearly 30 series at different stages of production were showcased during the 6th edition of TV Beats which reflected not only the giant leap forward quality-wise of drama making in the Baltics, but also the ability of the event to attract top-of-their-class producers, distributors, creators and programmers from around the world.

The Tallinn Black Nights Film Festival’s industry sidebar Industry@Tallinn & Baltic Event closes on Friday.
